#3876. "I feel that sense of responsibility more acutely": After BioWare's closure, the makers of a new Mass Effect 3 co-op remaster mod look to carry their legacy

"It's like watching a friend lose a parent - maybe you're not attached, but you feel the secondhand distress"

It appears I was premature in suggesting that the closure of BioWare might quickly spell an end for Mass Effect 3's strangely good, preposterously enduring co-op mode. I reinstalled and logged on just last week, and easily found a series of packed lobbies. Still, it was always regrettable that 2021's Mass Effect Legendary Edition opted not to remaster this multiplayer component alongside its dolled-up main trilogy, thus failing to introduce to a new generation the joys of performing teleporting psychic headbutts as a millennia-old bipedal frog.

This oversight has now been addressed, with the release of the Legendary Edition Multiplayer mod for said remaster. It's both a reconstruction and a slight expansion of ME3 multi, built in secret since 2023 by the ME3Tweaks group: a modding collective who've previously imbued the Legendary Edition with Mass Effect 1's Pinnacle Station DLC. It's also, some of its makers tell me, a bittersweet expression of appreciation for a series that looks unlikely to continue after EA's Mass Effect 5 cancellation.

At least some of that affection can be seen in how Legendary Edition Multiplayer differs from the already-available LEMP mod, which uses AI vibecoding to slap a mechanically identical recreation of ME3's co-op into the Legendary Edition's ones and zeroes. ME3Tweaks's version instead adds, according to member and longtime ME modder Audemus, a "completely overhauled UI, rebaked level lighting, upscaled and redrawn textures, upgraded shaders, native LE features such as HDR and controller support, networking and server replication improvements, extensive bug fixes, and entirely new wave modes such as Unified and Coalition."

Unified mode, for instance, quite literally mixes up ME3's enemy factions by forming mishmashed waves of baddies from across the Geth, Reaper, and Cerberus armies, thereby dusting off and stamping on your 14-year-old battle tactics. The mod also offers the ability to use ME3Tweaks' own servers for matchmaking, though a private server option remains for scraps with mates.

I'll definitely be giving this a try, once I'm back from my current travels. Though as with those OG ME3 multiplayer sessions last week, it'll be with a certain glumness, knowing that – despite a vocal campaign to give Mass Effect 5 a reprieve– I'll be playing something that had its future cut short.

The circumstances aren't lost on Legendary Edition Multiplayer's creators. "BioWare's closure is an incredibly sad moment for the games industry, and a particularly heartbreaking thing for the Mass Effect fanbase to contend with," Audemus tells me over email. "I feel as though our responsibility as a modding community has always been to carry the torch for this franchise, with or without an official future for it. But now that the future of Mass Effect has never been more in question, I feel that sense of responsibility more acutely than I ever have before."

Mgamerz, another modder on the project, recalls how "The day BioWare closed it didn't hit me until later in the day, a sort of numbness I can't really describe. I've spent 14 years working on their games - it's like watching a friend lose a parent - maybe you're not attached, but you feel the secondhand distress."

For some Legendary Edition Multiplayer modders, the affected BioWare staff included developers they knew personally. ME3Tweaks had previously been invited to embargoed discussions with both BioWare and EA on game modding, and Mass Effect writer and director Mac Walters (who left BioWare voluntarily in 2023) allegedly advocated for an even closer relationship.

"It's a shame to see it shut down," Mgamerz says. "Everyone speculated about it, but I know from talking to people internally there, that nobody knew the guillotine was about to drop." [Owners EA say the decision was only made after "months of planning, review, and analysis", though independent reporting suggests it was largely down to a straight choice between making ME5 or Star Wars Battlefront 3.]

"When we had our NDA with BioWare (since expired), apparently Mac Walters pushed internally to get my dev team brought into the manifold," he adds. "I say this as 'apparently', cause due to scheduling issues we never got to speak with Mac. But secondhand stories tell me he was a big proponent of modders - something that I would have loved to see more publicly shown.

"It is disappointing to know that the people who helped build the world my work now builds upon were killed unceremoniously - a problem that plagues the industry, and what kept me from further pursuing entry into it, something I used to dream of doing when I was younger."

RPS lawyers are telling me to tell you that nobody was literally killed. All the same, and even as someone much more familiar with playing the Mass Effects than tinkering around in their engine bays, the ME3Tweaks team make relatable points: we can frolick around an uprezzed Firebase Hydro, biotically biffing half-robot Turians like it's 2012, but it'll be hard not to look at all those conspicuous waist-high walls and think about the people who put them there. The same's true of having your mind drift to thoughts of their successors.

But there's another way of looking at it, which is that mods like Legendary Edition Multiplayer can preserve and maintain an original developer's work well beyond what their leveraged-buyout executive overlords might deem financially inconvenient. "I hope," as Audemus puts it, "that this mod - along with the fact that we've been able to build the technology to make mods like this in the first place - sends a message that there is incredible value in this franchise, and a passionate fanbase that is not ready to say goodbye to this universe and these games."

#3875. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel fans ponder split timelines, alternative histories, and more as story speculation runs wild following latest teaser

Following the release of yesterday's brief new The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel teaser trailer, story speculation is running rampant across communities dedicated to the fantasy series, with fans theorising everything from alternative histories to split timelines.

Yesterday's teaser - which arrived as part of Bethesda's 40th anniversary celebrations and comes amid devastating cuts across Xbox's first-party studios - was minimal. It opened with a shot of desert sand, before revealing the subtitle 'Sentinel' and ending with a quote from an unknown character. It's not much to go on, but is proving just enough to encourage discussion around what may be in store for Bethesda's next RPG.

And a good place to start is that quote. "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes," it reads. "A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate." All this is attributed to Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell, , but some fans think the accompanying date - 4E 206 - might be just as significant.

"[Sentinel] likely takes place five or more years after the start of Skyrim," hypothesised Reddit user 04nc1n9. "Hammerfell is a monarchy, it hasn't changed to any other political system after their imperial secession. The monarchy of Hammerfell has a Moth Priest on hand, even though the Moth Priests are generally an Imperial thing. Hammerfell's monarch has access to an Elder Scroll after the Elder Scrolls scattered."

This unexpected link between Moth Priests and Hammerfell's High Queen has created speculation of its own. One theory, combined with the proximity of Sentinel's story to that of Skyrim, has the Thalmor play a key role. "[It's] likely the Thalmor being the antagonists with so little time having passed," wrote user Jonesketi, "and with justifiable knowledge of how to cause great harm with the Elder Scrolls, [this] would've prompted [Hammerfell] to begin their own preparations. [The Thalmor are] also such a fitting antagonist since we didn't get to kick them down in Skyrim, which would offer catharsis if it came in Sentinel."

As for the quote itself, its vague wording has inspired some particularly out-there speculation. Some fans are looking back to previously vanquished forces in the series, in light of the phrase "a victory undone", and are theorising it might refer to a Dragon Break - an in-universe timeline split in which multiple events can all occur and simultaneously be true once the timelines reconverge. In previous games, Dragon Breaks have served as a handy explanation for the multiple endings.

Talk of "undone" events set user Wafelze's mind to the Numidium, a giant mechanical golem whose activation in The Elder Scrolls 2: Daggerfall caused its own Dragon Break. "With how important time is to Skyrim’s story," they speculated, "it wouldn’t surprise me if this story is about time being entirely broken."

"See, I'm thinking it has to do with the creation of Nirn and Lorkhan," wrote Potential Film 7140. "The Altmer hate Lorkhan and men see the creation of the world as a victory. The elves did not ... maybe they'll try to undo what created the divines so they can go back to their original ancestry. Wildly out-there take but that's what my brain tells me."

What's more, the theories around split timelines and the Thalmor have converged with thoughts of a possible 'Man in the High Castle'-style alternate history setting for Sentinel, unfolding in a version of the world where the Thalmor have power. "Maybe the Empire originally held together after Oblivion, and the Thalmor used some cheater Elder Scroll magic to rewrite history so that they dunked on the Empire," suggested Original League 6094. "Or if I recall, Hammerfell was doing a great job beating the Thalmor as of Skyrim. Maybe the version of events got overwritten and now Hammerfell is under Thalmor subjugation, and the Elder Scroll is giving her glimpses of the timeline where Hammerfell won."

Will these theories prove to be true? With the launch of Sentinel still reportedly years away, it could be some time before we find out. But if nothing else, this feverish story speculation suggests there's a major hunger among fans for information - any information - about Sentinel. And that's no real surprise. After all, yesterday's teaser was only the second official look at a game whose reveal has been dragging on for over eight years now.

#3874. Beholder IV announced for PC

Alawar has announced Beholder IV, the latest installment in its dystopian narrative series, as part of the franchise’s 10th anniversary celebrations. It will be available for PC via Steam.

The announcement is accompanied by the release of the new digital comic, Beholder: The Landlord’s Handbook, and a 90 percent-off discount on the original Beholder.

Here is an overview of Beholder IV, via its Steam page:

From the creators of Beholder: Conductor.

Beholder IV returns to a totalitarian State where your choices matter. Live a double life as an official and underground agent. Spy, sabotage, build relationships, and decide others’ fates. But brace for a knock: the police are coming, and your home is full of evidence.

You used to watch your tenants, peer through keyholes, and report those who fell foul of the State. Now everything has changed.

You are a young Ministry official. Diligent, promising, and loyal to the State. At least, that’s what your superiors believe.

In truth, you work for the underground. You steal classified documents, sabotage operations, and help the resistance. But there’s something you’re hiding even from your comrades.

Welcome to the Ministry! Here, you’ll process citizens’ files, sign orders, and steadily climb the career ladder. But your real work begins when you leave your desk.

Every employee has their own routine, weaknesses, and secrets. And your assignments won’t lead you to all of them. Sometimes, you just need to be in the right place at the right time.

By day, you serve the State. In secret, you work for those who dream of destroying it.

The Ministry orders you to find a traitor among your colleagues. The underground asks you to help that same person escape. Your superior offers a promotion that will grant you access to classified archives. But your new position will require you to sign arrest orders yourself. Where will your loyalties lie?

Carry out assignments for both sides, gather intelligence, prepare underground operations, and decide whom to help. The State isn’t always wrong, the resistance isn’t always right, and your own interests may matter more than either cause.

Your workday is over. You return home with stolen documents—and suddenly, there’s a knock at the door. The police are here to search your apartment. You have seconds to hide the evidence of your double life.

With every search, the police become more persistent. One day, they may arrive knowing exactly what they’re looking for.

You’re used to looking inside other people’s closets. Now try to keep everyone out of yours.

Even in a world of total control, there’s room for love. But trusting someone here is more dangerous than it seems.

Meet four very different women. Get to know their personalities, help them with personal problems, flirt, go on dates, and develop romantic relationships. Some work for the State; others belong to the resistance. Each has her own beliefs, desires, and secrets.

But what happens if the woman you love ends up on the other side? Or asks you to do something that goes against your orders?

In Beholder IV, there’s no “do the right thing” button.

You can save someone from arrest—or sign the order that ruins their life. You can help the resistance carry out an operation or secretly hand its plans to the State.

Steal the document you need. Alter a patrol schedule. Warn someone of danger. Or simply do nothing.

The game will remember your actions. Your decisions affect characters’ fates, relationships, the course of operations, and how the story unfolds. On your next playthrough, things could turn out very differently.

A loyal revolutionary? A ruthless careerist? A double agent using both sides for personal gain? A resistance leader? Or perhaps an oligarch in the service of the State? Or someone willing to betray them all for the answer to a single question?

Uncover the truth in Beholder IV—a new chapter in the dark dystopian series where everyone is watching everyone else. And now, they’re watching you.

I've been playing Path of Exile for almost ten years and have put a ton of hours into PoE2 since it entered early access, and in all that time there's one feature that I've wished for more than any other. More than stash tabs, more than fancy microtransactions, even more than finally finding a mirror in the wild.

What I want more than anything is a death recap: a way to finally have some idea why my turbo powerful character that's blasting through a map went pop. At an interview at ExileCon this weekend, game director Jonathan Rogers confirmed that it's finally coming to Path of Exile 2.

I don't know whether Grinding Gear intended to announce the feature this weekend, but during the keynote's live demo of new content, Mark Roberts' character died. And there before our eyes, live and in person, was a death recap screen. After we all got done cheering, Rogers laughed and confirmed that the feature was present and would be included in the full 1.0 release coming up on December 11.

"I was really worried that it wasn't going to be useful enough or accurate enough, but we got it to a place that I'm fairly happy with," Rogers said when I asked him to confirm that the feature would be present at launch.

"The thing that's not quite good is the damage over time tracking," he added. "We do tell you that you took it but we don't know where it came from.”

Thankfully, it's a bit easier to parse taking damage over time in the game already, and he assured us that they're working on getting that sorted out as well.

One of the reasons that the death recap is such an important feature is that it can be incredibly hard to parse exactly what you should be focusing on with your character once you get to the endgame. A lot of times you've maxed your resistances, have a decent life pool, and a good amount of either armour, evasion, or energy shield, but still something comes along and explodes you. And since there are often many monsters on the screen, to say nothing of all the explosions or arrows or minions or ice comets that you yourself are spamming, it can be almost impossible to figure out what happened.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

"The most important thing to be was like… here's the damage you took and how much of it was mitigated," says Rogers. "My goal was to drive you toward 'what is the thing I need to fix about my character to have avoided this.'" A big physical hit? Maybe some more evasion or life. Cold damage? Maybe grab a couple jewels with + to max cold res.

Sometimes though, the problem isn't with you. Sometimes you get a killer crab that kills hundreds of thousands of players due to a typo. He thinks the death recap will help here, too.

"This may sound a bit funny, but I think it'll actually give our players an avenue to complain about the correct things. Sometimes we just have monsters that have wrong balance values, it happens, and in the heat of battle you don't know what it was. Now you'll be able to say this particular monster is the one that has the damage that's off the hook and then it allows them to direct us to that."

Despite having their own internal systems to monitor monster behavior, nothing beats the urgency and immediacy of a legion of players crying out at once on the internet about killer crabs.

Mark Roberts went on to say that he anticipates that the feature "will 100% be asked for en masse" by Path of Exile 1 players, and if it is, they'll port that functionality over as soon as they can.

As for me, the death recap is but one of many amazing features I'm looking forward to in Path of Exile 2's full release. It will be available on December 11th.

Russ has been playing PC games since the top of the line graphics were in ASCII and has been obsessed with them just about as long. After a coordinated influence campaign to bamboozle his parents into getting a high speed internet connection to play EverQuest, his fate was well and truly sealed. When he's not writing about videogames, he's teaching karate, cooking an overly complicated dish, or attempting to raise his daughter with a well rounded classical education (Civilization, Doom, and Baldur's Gate, of course). He's probably mapping in Path of Exile right now.

#3872. God of War Laufey delayed three months to May 2027, as Sony Santa Monica escapes a packed February

"We will make the most of each moment until then."

God of War Laufey has been delayed. Sony Santa Monica's PS5 exclusive is now dodging the crowded month of February and will instead come out on 20th May, 2027.

Developer Sony Santa Monica announced it's pushing back the upcoming action epic via a brief social media post. While the studio stopped short of giving a reason for the delay, it did say it's using the extra time to polish Faye's solo adventure.

"Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we've been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye's journey through the Everywhen. We don't take for granted the trust placed in the studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans," the studio wrote.

"With this in mind, we've made the decision to delay God of War Laufey's release to May 20th, 2027," the statement continued. "We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential. On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we'll be back to share more updates soon."

God of War Laufey is notably the first game in the famed PlayStation series to not star Kratos in the lead role. This time around, Faye takes the lead through a version of the afterlife that houses gods and deities from multiple mythologies - and it's bringing back the original series' faster combat, too.

Of course, Kratos will return in future God of War games (he also shows up here and there during Faye's romp), and whatever that next Kratos game becomes, it'll supposedly connect to the events of Laufey, according to the developer.

On the bright side, the delay might be good news for anyone worried about their impossibly large and ever expanding backlogs. February 2027 is already packed with really exciting games - from the Fable reboot and Persona 4 Revival to Metro 2039. Hopefully, Laufey's delay gives everyone more breathing room.

#3871. Path of Exile 2's 1.0 version is out this year after all, arriving in December with a full campaign, two neat new classes, and more

About a year ago, the devs behind Path of Exile 2 delayed the game's 1.0 release to an unspecified point in time, only offering the hope that it wouldn't slip into 2027 (doing much the same about half a year later). But there's good news: it won't! As the action RPG now has a 1.0 release date locked in, alongside a look at what you can expect when it arrives.

As shared by developer Grinding Gear Games, Path of Exile 2 will be launching into 1.0 next month on December 11th. Probably the biggest aspect of the update is the fact that the game's campaign will be completely playable, with the fifth and sixth acts being added in wrapping up the story that's been built up over its early access release. You'll also have two new classes to play around with, if you've gotten bored of the ones you've tried so far or just fancy something new.

The first is the Shadow, which appropriately introduces a stealth mechanic. As you might expect of such a class, while you're in stealth, "monsters can't see you until you get within a short distance of them." Being in said mode also bolsters your dagger with a range of bonuses, and the Shadow also has another weapon type available to them, traps. You prepare these in stealth, "then trigger them automatically as you strike. Traps explode in the order they were thrown, allowing you to set up the perfect combo!" And the other class is the Duelist, who has the new stance mechanic. This lets you strengthen your sword skills, "enhancing each of them in different ways," with various stances allowing for "even deadlier combinations."

Beyond that, there's a new league to try out that lets you team up with Varek and his mercs to "conquer Wraeclast!" A whole bunch of new items have been added in, with many being revamped, and you'll also find new skills gems and support gems reworked. The passive skill tree has also seen a makeover, and a number of classes have also received some improvements. You can read about all of that in more detail right here.

Metallica and Korn are doing huge sellout tours, Godzilla is stomping through cinemas, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is the hottest game going. It's 1998 all over again. The latter's really leaving a mark, moving the needle on Switch 2 sales to a considerable degree, thanks to that sweet limited edition console.

Some analysis comes from Mat Piscatella, who is the senior director and video game industry advisor and analytics firm Circana. On Bluesky, he posts about how Link's classic adventure to save Hyrule impacted the Switch 2's performance in the US.

The Legend of Zelda: 40th Anniversary Edition console helped drive total US Switch 2 hardware dollar sales to its highest weekly total of 2026 to date (w/e Oct 31, 2026). Total US video game hardware spending jumped 81% in the week compared to a year ago. Source: Circana Retail Tracking Service

Absolutely no surprises there, right? That's the kind of thing Nintendo lives for, and there are a lot of dedicated fans who happily engage in such things. Heck, I've never been attracted to limited versions of consoles, but even I felt the pull for that Zelda one. It's such a nice aesthetic.

#3869. "This trailer is my way of saying goodbye": Have a listen to the Mass Effect 5 score that could have been, courtesy of one of the original games' composers

By this point I'm probably safe in assuming that you all know EA are shutting down BioWare, and that Mass Effect 5 has been cancelled in turn. You may have also seen that an internal trailer for Mass Effect 5, or Universe as it was seemingly going to be called, was leaked not long after the news broke, and that Sam Hulick, one of the composers on the original trilogy of games, shared he was going to offer up his re-scored version of the trailer. Well, it's N7 Day, as rough as that will be for many of the developers on the game, but Hulick has stood by his word, and shared an oral glimpse at what the world of Mass Effect Universe could have sounded like.

You can check out this new version of the trailer below, perhaps pop it on while you have a read of the rest of this post, as Hulick did also write in a Patreon blog about his experience with the series. "As part of my own closure, and as a love letter to the fans, I really wanted to re-score the leaked Mass Effect Universe trailer in time for N7 Day this year," he wrote. "BioWare edited a killer track called “Quartz” by French 79 to fit their trailer, which I think hinted at a slight directional shift in the score. Using that as inspiration, along with the musical tone from my work on the first three Mass Effect games, I hit the studio and got to work."

As it turns out, BioWare had actually reached out to Hulick asking him to potentially do some work for the project. "This year, BioWare emailed me asking if I was interested in working with them on an internal demo, and they said they were 'hoping to get some music written that would feel like Mass [Effect], supporting our new direction.' Of course, I said yes!" This doesn't mean he wouldn't have composed the actual game, as a composer hadn't been officially selected, but Hulick said he was "more than happy to collaborate on the new game’s musical direction and help make their internal demo sound as good as it could."

Hulick also spoke of some of the ideas he had for the direction Mass Effect Universe's soundtrack could take, noting how he "thought it would’ve been incredible to bring more songs with lyrics into the game," considering how many people loved the first game's end-credits song. "This would’ve been a great way to highlight more emotional moments in the narrative. Artists at the top of my collaboration list included Gunship, NINA, and The Midnight, all of whom have a moody, cinematic synthwave vibe that would’ve meshed well with the score in my head. And I’m pretty sure the Gunship guys are gamers, and if they’re Mass Effect fans, that would’ve been the icing on the cake!"

Of course, with the studio now closing, this never got to go very far, the news hitting Hulick "particularly hard, as the Mass Effect trilogy is a core part of my origin story as a composer." For the composer, ultimately "this trailer is my way of saying goodbye… at least for now." This continues to be a horrendously sad moment in the industry! As always, solidarity with the team at BioWare.

#3868. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's Navi actor reprises her role after 28 years, but it was a total accident due to Nintendo's blind auditions

For The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's shiny new remake, Nintendo unintentionally cast the same actor twice - 28 years apart - to deliver Navi's infamous "Heys!" and "Listens!"

The Switch 2's Ocarina of Time makes a pretty substantial change to the N64's Ocarina of Time, released almost three decades prior. There's proper voice acting this time, of course - not just grunts and murmurs and hyahs. But even when retroactively adding new things, Nintendo wanted to ensure the remake's cast matched the original's pretty faithfully, so the developer held blind auditions that eventually paved the way for one actor to reprise their role during Link's adventure.

"We felt that if we were going to improve the graphics so dramatically, the cutscenes needed to be fully voiced to match," director HokWai Ng explained in the most recent Ask The Developer blog. "But at the same time, we knew we shouldn't mess with established perceptions of how certain characters sound based on the original. Navi's "Listen!" is one example. Even someone who's never played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time may have heard it before. We absolutely didn't want to change anything as iconic as that."

To maintain the original's nostalgic sounds and voices, Nintendo held blind auditions with the goal of finding actors who could recreate the "feel of the original game."

Series director Eiji Aonuma recalls that the team wanted to choose actors "based solely on which voices most closely resembled those of the original." And, who woulda guessed? "As fate would have it, one of the actors we selected had actually voiced the same character in the Nintendo 64 version. None of us saw that coming."

The duo didn't outright name which character they're talking about, but fans have long been speculating that Kaori Mizuhashi might be reprising her role as Link's trusty fairy companion Navi - at least, in the Japanese language version. A leaked online video of the game's credits now also confirms that Mizuhashi is back almost three decades later. I suppose it only makes sense that the person who most closely resembles Navi is Navi.

Chris Donlan called the new version an "astonishing remake" in his five-star Eurogamer Ocarina of Time review.

Wardogs enjoyed an incredible launch, but Season 2 was very much Bulkhead's 'difficult second album' phase of live service development. A cash-incentive experiment to rebalance the game's weaker blue team was dropped just one day it went live, while the studio's broader attempt to address player concerns ended up sucking a lot of the fun out of the military FPS.

Now, with Season 3 on the horizon, Bulkhead has addressed the mistakes the studio made with Season 2 and discussed how the new season will address them. It's a tale that involves a new map, new modes, new upgrade paths, and an AI-powered anticheat.

The Road to Season 3 video kicks off with a mea culpa from Bulkhead. "Whilst learning to adapt to running a live service, we decided with good intent to try to respond to negative reviews with actions rather than words," Howard Philpott, Bulkhead's UI/UX director, says in the video. "When the patch notes dropped, on paper the reaction was great. But in reality, when the season went live, the sentiment went quickly downhill.

Bulkhead believes the changes it made were too aggressive, while the studio was too easily swayed by the whims of vocal players and its own worries about the inevitable post-launch player dropoff. Henceforth, Bulkhead intends to stick to its guns. "No matter how incredible the launch was for us and players, both we, the developers and you as players must hold strong and not speedrun fixes to appease the loudest voices."

With that said, Season 3 brings several hopefully more considered changes to Wardogs. First up is a new map called Sabatulo. With a heavier focus on urban environments than existing Wardogs battlegrounds, Sabatulo is designed to facilitate more close-quarters fights than other maps, giving you more reason to equip shorter-range weaponry.

Arguably more significant, however, is multi-track unlocks. Rather than locking every unlock behind a specific role, Bulkhead has adjusted progression so that any item that might feasibly be used by a role can be unlocked by playing it. This is something of a stopgap solution, as Bulkhead works on a bigger rework to progression coming in 2027. But it should mean players no longer have to grind roles they don't want to play to get the items they need.

Alongside these progression tweaks, Season 3 introduces a new "Limited" mode, which removes high-tier weapons, armour, vehicles etc from the roster. The idea is to level the playing field so that more casual players can enjoy the game without getting constantly murked by fully kitted out super-soldiers. It's a sensible option to include, and I'll be intrigued to see how popular it proves.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Finally, Season 3 heralds the arrival of what Bulkhead claims to be "one of the world's most sophisticated anti-cheat systems", which the studio has produced by "analysing 187 million hours of gameplay with the assistance of machine learning and AI". Apparently, the system went live when the video was published, banning a whopping 185,000 accounts as it did so.

Apparently, Bulkhead planned to launch this system later in Wardogs' life, but the game's sheer popularity has given them the data they require to implement it much earlier. "In order for us to train our models, we needed to let cheaters go through their journey of refining and tuning their cheats so we could see them evolve," says Bulkhead CEO Joe Brammer. "This method has given us time to analyse and build consistent case reports confirming cheaters who were attempting to hide in the dark."

To touch upon the AI element, obviously it's a loaded term nowadays (and, usually, rightly so) but this kind of targeted, homebrew machine learning is not necessarily the same flavour of AI as the multipurpose LLMs that are ruining everything from emails to greetings cards. Brammer says that the system won't eliminate cheaters completely, and that cheating will always be a problem "unless governments start criminalising cheat development"—which is a very Brammer thing to say. But the studio seems confident that the system will help produce a better play experience when Season 3 arrives on November 12.

#3866. County of Fortune, now out in early access, is a medieval city builder that asks, why limit yourself to just one city?

Don't count your towns before they've hatched

I know what you want. The humble city builder isn't enough for you any more, is it? You need a cities builder, you can't just stop at one, but you don't want to build up an entirely different city on a new save file. If it were up to you, they'd all be on the same map, a motorway's worth of a drive away from each other. If we're talking contemporary cities, I can't help you, but if you can settle for numerous medieval towns across an entire county, then County of Fortune should do just fine.

County of Fortune just landed in early access a couple of days ago, and as mentioned (and as the name suggests), you're building up an entire county! "You place whole settlements across the county and lay each one out on a medieval grid. Each one grows, specializes, and knits into a living region where rivers and resources decide what thrives," the game's Steam page explains. "As the county matures, a second game begins. Named mayors run each settlement. Rival noble houses weave politics across the region. And migrating cultures bless some villages, while complicating others."

To start with, it's up to you where you want to place each of your settlements, deciding how they individually function as you do. The towns are then partially procedurally generated as they get built up, slowly connecting to other nearby towns. "The scale is the point. You are not zooming into a single town - you are zooming out to see a whole county come to life." A big part of the strategy comes down to how you navigate the map; finding resource deposits, picking appropriate terrain profiles, utilising rivers efficiently, finding a good climate, setting good trade routes, it's all about working with the land you've got.

Each settlement will produce different things depending on the materials available to them in close proximity, meaning each one has a unique function. You've got different types of characters to consider too: mayors, noble houses and cultures, all intersecting with different elements of how a town functions. Seems like a unique approach to city building! And as mentioned, it's out in early access; you can pick it up on Steam here.

Conversely, Shawn Layden says he's "never seen a good game built by committee"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's the "creative genius" of auteurs like Hideo Kojima that's responsible for "games we always remember," according to former PlayStation boss Shawn Layden, who says he's "never seen a good game built by committee."

Speaking on The Trophy Room podcast (below), Layden – former president and CEO of Sony Interactive Entertainment America as well as chairman of SIE Worldwide Studios – is asked if the games industry "overvalues" auteurs, with host Joe Moran specifically pointing to Metal Gear and Death Stranding's Hideo Kojima, BioShock's Ken Levine, The Last of Us's Neil Druckmann, and Todd Howard of The Elder Scrolls and Fallout fame.

Clearly, though, Layden doesn't think so. "Look, you know, there was only one Rembrandt, right?" he begins. "And there's only one Martin Scorsese. Auteurs, quote unquote, built this business."

As far as Layden is concerned, he "sadly" believes that "quite often greatness requires a megalomaniac. It just does." He refers to PlayStation's creator as he adds: "This is a guy who worked for Ken Kutaragi, so I know what I'm talking about."

Ultimately, it comes down to games being memorable, and the games from those auteurs being excellent examples. "From that chaotic genius comes games we always remember," Layden says. "I've never seen a good game built by committee. I've seen a lot of bad games built by committee, but I won't name them here. And that's just kind of how it is."

From his time at PlayStation, Layden notes that the goals of the big bosses like himself and the auteurs behind them were ultimately "the same" – to make a "great game." He continues: "My job as chairman of the studios is just to get the rocks out of the road, lift the logs off the road. When Tokyo or headquarters starts calling, 'I'll take that call. You guys keep working on the game.'" All of this is to "protect the auteurs" from potential "distractions."

While Kojima is the game creator probably most frequently cited as an auteur, the description arguably applies to a whole bunch of notable devs – just think of the likes of Nier's Yoko Taro or FromSoftware boss Hidetaka Miyazaki. It's hard to imagine where we'd be without the innovation pushed by devs like them – and long may that continue.

#3864. Arkane union says closing the studio "would probably be more expensive" for Xbox than simply finishing Marvel's Blade

"Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic."

Xbox would probably spend more money shutting down Arkane Lyon than it would trying to finish and release Marvel's Blade, according to a union representing workers from the beloved imsim studio.

In a statement posted to the STJV (Syndicat des travailleureuses du jeu vidéo) website, the French union claimed that development on Marvel's Blade is "going fine" and is shaping up to be on par with Arkane's widely acclaimed gameography. By choosing to part ways with and potentially close the famed studio, the union says Microsoft is "sabotaging the game it funded."

After Xbox's sweeping job cuts and divestments from several first-party studios, Arkane was recently given until December to find a new buyer and ensure its future. Ubisoft Entertainment (Assassin's Creed, Rainbow Six) is reportedly one of the companies interested in buying the studio behind Dishonored, Prey and the upcoming superhero adaptation, though nothing has been finalised yet.

The union also blamed many of the studio's problems on Microsoft - a hiring freeze that lasted more than a year supposedly inflated the game's budget and caused additional internal delays. "Microsoft now use those same delay and additional costs as a reason to close the studio," the statement said.

"Even this closure itself is done against any financial logic, as closing Arkane today would probably be more expensive than finishing the game," it continued. "The truth is that Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic, in which our lives, projects and dreams are voided, so we can better serve Microsoft's short term financial goals[...] The decision to close Arkane is solely the brutal application of a never-ending search for maximum profit optimization. Arkane is profitable. Just not profitable for Microsoft."

The union's list of demands now asks for employees to be able to have a say in choosing a potential buyer, as well as protections against any layoffs that might happen in the next few years. Should acquisition talks fail, the union claimed that the resources in Microsoft's redundancy package are "outrageously low" - so it's also demanding a redundancy payment of €200,000 per employee and further support.

Arkane's not the only developer reeling from Xbox's cuts. Double Fine (Psychonauts), Compulsion Games (South of Midnight) and Undead Labs (State of Decay) all managed to buy their independence, but had to lay off some staff as a result. It's not looking good for Hellblade developer Ninja Theory, either.

#3863. Echoes of Mirror's Edge, Dishonored and a dream set in Italy I once had can be found in Boars in Rome, an expressive parkour platformer set in dystopian Rome

Years ago, I had this dream where I was parkouring through a greatly sunken version of Venice, no doubt sourced from the many hours I put into Assassin's Creed 2 as a teen who should have been studying for their GCSEs a lot more than they were. It's stuck with me after all this time mostly because of how much I wanted to capture that feeling again somehow, as the real Assassin's Creed didn't quite cut it. And lo and behold, there I was today browsing Bluesky when I came across Boars in Rome, a Mirror's Edge and Counter Strike Surf inspired parkour platformer set in a dystopian version of Rome.

Truthfully, witnessing the clip I've shared below was baffling to me. "This is what I dreamt of!" More or less, anyway, for the setting isn't quite the same; "You have been selected to start a new life off planet. Earth has been abandoned," explains the game's Steam page. "Machines keep working and nature claims what remains. Find out what happened while you were frozen in time by exploring the remnants of Rome where historical monuments mix with futurist megastructures."

Mirrors Edge x Counter Strike Surf where you parkour on anything! Be smooth n stylish in dystopian Rome. Or just jump around and explore, whatever works for you. It's called Boars in Rome! #PitchYaGame[image or embed]

Not all of it matches that dream of mine, some of it leans much more into brutalism than the typical, much older architecture you'd expect of Rome, but it's there nonetheless. In motion, Boars in Rome feels quite oneiric too. There is so much more control over the game's avatar than what my real body is capable of, or wants to do. You can run, jump, slide and wallrun, positioning it quite closely to VHOLUME mechanically. Where it differs is in its additives, movement tech like being able to swing on lampposts or vault over low down obstacles.

VHOLUME is more of a game about providing you with a simple toolkit and leaving you to push it to its maximum. Boars in Roam is a touch more expressive, and I'd dare to even call it an immersive sim. The levels you can romp around are linear, you have an end point to reach, only the journey is up to you. It certainly feels appropriate to put it in the im sim camp given that, at least the game's first level, calls to mind Viktor Antonov's work on Dishonored (and Half-Life 2, too, honestly).

As it currently stands, there's no release date for Boars in Rome, but there is a playtest you can sign up and gain immediate access to if you fancy a go yourself; you can do so on Steam right here, or at least pop it a wishlist.

Aurbis converts Bethesda's fantasy adventure into a shared multiplayer world, with all the systems that entails.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

PC gaming isn't short of multiplayer fantasy adventures these days, but there is still something alluring about the idea of playing Skyrim with pals. Some mods have facilitated small-scale Skyrim multiplayer in the past, like the cooperative mod Skyrim Together. But Aurbis goes several step further, converting Bethesda's RPG into a persistent online roleplaying server—essentially a Skyrim MMO in all but name.

According to its ModDB page, Aurbis transforms Skyrim's solo adventure into "a persistent world where player actions create lasting consequences", snythesising Skyrim's existing experience with a bunch of multiplayer and MMO-like systems. It's designed with roleplaying in mind, though the mod's creators stress that RP is not mandatory, and players can focus on other elements like cooperative dungeon runs or PvP play if they so choose.

The list of changes and additions to Aurbis is impressive, running from character creation outward. The retooled character builder is designed to let avatars "develop over time instead of becoming powerful immediately", though it also lets players start with vampirism or lycanthropy for roleplaying purposes.

Those roles are heavily defined by the player's choice of Birthsign, which affects how efficiently skills develop. Crafting professions are supported by a player-driven economy that factors in bank accounts, property ownership and player-created quests, while activities like combat are designed to be dangerous and reward "preparation, equipment, specialisation and teamwork."

Alongside these changes are entirely new, multiplayer specific systems. Players can form their own groups called Cohorts, designed to act as a "strong foundation for MMO-style social gameplay". This ranges from establishing parties and guilds to aligning yourself with Skyrim's existing factions, combining "familiar Skyrim content with custom multiplayer mechanics".

The list doesn't end there, either. There are more nuanced survival systems, complex horse management, MMO style death penalties, and much more. There's even a fully-fledged language and literacy system whereby players "do not automatically understand every conversation or know every location", so mastering language and literacy can provide a genuine roleplaying advantage.

It sounds wild, and this only represents an early access release. If you fancy investigating Aurbis, all you need is a legitimate copy of Skyrim that's downgraded to version 1.6.1170. The beta is invite-only, but a session key is listed on the ModDB page that should grant you access, while Aurbis has a custom launcher that downloads and maintains all required mods.

#3861. The Sunday Papers

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

Sundays are for waking up covered in sand. The roof of your house is missing. A small man stands in the emptied bed of a dump truck. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6," he says. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6," he repeats. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6," he declares once again, beginning to move towards you this time. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6." You realise your hands are tied down. Oh no.

Is he about to sit on your face? WAIT, THAT'S NOW ILLEGAL HERE IN THE UK. NO, PLEASE, DON'T SIT ON MY-time seems to slow as the bare backside approaches your visage. As its cheeks prepare to become as sandy as yours, you hear its wielder say: "And we thought, hey, given the moment..."

Panicking, you scrabble for anything to say which might free you before something that might get a British MP's hackles up can occur. "Things first went awry when I turned up for my appointment to find a tall German man wearing a cowboy hat asking a PR if he could play the game," you blurt out. The posterior momentarily stops moving towards you. Buoyed, you continue to tell a story you heard from VGC's Chris Scullion.

I was asked if I minded sharing my one-to-one appointment with this chap too, to which my inherent British cowardly courtesy kicked in and I lied that it was perfectly fine.

"I want drums", he said as he entered the room. "We are playing Dani California by Red Hot Chili Peppers." Rather than ask him whether he also fancied telling me where I was going for dinner later, I picked up my guitar and went along with it, eager to just play the game.

The bottom begins its agonising crawl towards your kisser once more. You can feel the occupants of parliamentary benches begin to sense a disturbance in the force. Maybe if you can make the bumholder sad, that'll do the trick. You try to remember how Sebastian Cardoso of Game Studio Unlocked's presentation on the tragic fates of game studios after acquisitions went.

A hundred and twenty-three of the 362 developers were shut outright. The average life from acquisition to closure is 6.4 years and the median is 5, meaning half of all closed studios were dead within five years of their acquisition.

The familiar names mostly died fast. EA closed Pandemic two years after buying it. Sony shut Firewalk barely a year and a half in. Warner Bros. closed Player First roughly seven months after acquiring it. Bluepoint, closed at the five-year mark, is exactly what the median looks like.

It's no use. That arse's shadow its creeping across ever more of your face like your're a planet with a nose and it's the Vogon Constructor Fleet. Maybe you can somehow contort your head to the side. Arrrggghh. You call on all the strength of muscles you barely ever use and think of the incredible gymnastic feats executed by Physical Contortion Gamer's Josh Wolens during an ongoing GTA diary series.

Attempting to do flips, then, just sort of rotates your entire body below the diaphragm while your head and chest area remain bolt upright, rigid in such a way that you could feasibly fly a flag from your own thorax.

Which looks odd. Nevertheless, it is pretty fun to scoot and roll your way through Los Santos. At one point, I attempted a double frontflip in the middle of a part of the map that had been deleted for some reason. It didn't quite work out, and I ended up colliding with and possibly killing a man in a fursuit.

It doesn't work. You can't get away. You begin to scream. The posterioperator stops repeating the words "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6". Instead, he asks where that mysterious German cowboy you mentioned earlier has gone. You don't have a clue, and can't help admitting as much. "Ah well." The derriere resumes its descent, now mere inches from your mug. This is the end. You have one last rummage through your mind for possible solutions.

Respec's Tom Orry hasn't managed to save you. "Fine, sit on my face and send me to hell," you shout into the pinkish ring of doom as British cops prepare to ram-raid your abode and arrest you for crimes against a prude's definition of acceptable shagging.

The bum stops. Its owner asks if you've just said the word Sentinel. "Yes," you lie.

The arse is raised and swapped for the face of a man. "What a perfect time for you to realise what The Elder Scrolls 6 is actually called," he says.

You notice he's not Todd Howard. Or Adrian Edmondson.

"It's Ade's month off and they needed another baldy to play this esteemed role," Sir Patrick Stewart announces, clearly responding the look of befuddlement your face can still have since it hasn't been crushed by a ten-tonne tush. You wonder how you didn't recognise his voice before, especially given he played the emperor in Oblivion.

"Here's to the next Bethesda game after Starfield," the Stew sings as the police bust through the door and he's beamed up before they can tackle him.

#3860. Valve explains why it's running behind on Steam game approvals, asks developers to perform basic release checks to prevent re-reviews

In the wake of witnessing an unprecedented number of game submissions to Steam over the last few months, Valve has been forced to delay approvals in order to deal with the existing backlog.

Following complaints by game developers on social media and elsewhere, Valve has now responded to explain why it's taking longer to get games approved. The short version: re-reviews are clogging up the system.

"We aim to test every game build in a timely manner, typically within three-five business days," Valve wrote in a Steam post. "However, we're running a little behind right now and taking up to 12 business days. Much of that delay is due to having to re-review games, which isn't great for you or for us."

As Valve explained in the post, games need to be re-reviewed when they're rejected for missing key quality assurance checks. In an effort to make it easier for developers to get it right the first time, Valve updated the Steam release checklist to include new, tighter requirements.

These include a requirement to run the game through Steam for at least five minutes. According to Valve, some of the games submitted have not been played through Steam.

"This means that even if a game runs smoothly when a dev launches their executable directly, they might have missed basic steps that would impact a user installing and playing via Steam," Valve explained.

Valve is also making it a rule to mention whether the game requires common redistributables such as DirectX, Visual C++, .NET, XNA. While Steam can automatically install many common redistributables, it needs to know which ones are needed (if any). There are also new rules about achievement readiness, cloud save detection, and some updates to Steam store page requirements.

"We now surface some of the most common issues we see missed, along with asking for some information to help our reviewers from the start," Valve added. "For example, if your game offers multiple languages and you've indicated that on your store page, we'll ask you to ensure you've included them in your build".

While Valve did not directly name gen-AI as a potential reason for this rise in the number of poor submissions, it's clear the Steam company needs to find a way to deal with the massive number of AI-assisted games.

Valve recently addressed Steam's AI game cloning problem by suggesting developers make their games less copyable. Incidentally, some of the developers whose game approvals are delayed now fear their games will be cloned by others using gen-AI and land a Steam page before the original article has made it out of submission.

#3859. Uh oh, Zelda fans have accidentally created a mix between kid and adult Link, and the result is hilarious

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time‘s remake is out, seemingly capturing the magic of the original and possibly even more. Fans have stumbled upon a puzzling new version of Link the developers definitely didn’t have in mind. Time to meet the new member of the Zelda family.

In the original Ocarina of Time, Link only ever gets the silver gauntlets chest as a child. In the remake, he’s only supposed to get it as a child as well, but he can actually get them as Adult Link via a glitch that triggers a very unique time paradox-like reaction.

Since Link’s only ever supposed to get these as an adult, getting them earlier on will cause the game to fit the adult Link’s model into the tiny one, a desperate move that will seriously impact his looks.

Using a glitch to get a really big jump in the remake, its now possible to get the silver gauntlets chest as adult, which is supposed to be gotten as child. The cutscene that plays after tries to fit adult link into child link model, which ends up looking like this. pic.twitter.com/un9DflnvxT

Some are calling this new creature “Child Adult Link,” others named him “Lunk.” but everyone is cherishing his miraculous birth, regardless of how unintentional it might’ve been.

Better yet, Lunk is seemingly not even the only new somewhat Link-shaped lifeform in the game. Some other fans have shared it’s also possible to create a reverse form of Lunk, which creates, ugh… Adult Child Link? Lank? I don’t know what to call it, and I don’t even know how you get to morph your Link into this other version. What I can definitely tell you is what you’ll be thinking as soon as you lay your eyes on it, which is that it also looks hilarious.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

And look, puberty is a strange phase for everyone. It’s actually completely normal that either “new” version of Link looks pretty awkward. There’s a reason why the original timeskips from kid Link into his adult version. Still, this accidental addition makes the remake even more nostalgic, as it can now remind the many of us who enjoyed the original during our strangest times that things would eventually turn out fine.

And, even if that’s not enough, there are even some fans who are liking “Lunk” for what he is, pointing out his resemblance to a very popular Internet figure.

Though Nintendo’s take on the remake’s aesthetic left the fan base considerably divided, this is exactly the kind of thing that the whole community will enjoy and possibly even elevate into an all-time meme—something all 10/10 games deserve.

You can now play the Zelda Ocarina of Time remake on the Nintendo Switch 2.

#3857. Despite hardware worries and rising costs, Sony says PlayStation 6 development is on track and "progressing as scheduled"

Today, Thursday 5th November, 2026, Sony shared its latest financial results, reporting on the second quarter of financial year 2026 for the company. In a wide-ranging set of statements, we learned that the company's overall profits have been charged by the box office success of Spider-Man: Brand New Day, and that its annual profit outlook has been raised following a particularly successful quarter.

As for PlayStation, Sony CFO Lin Tao hinted at the status of the PlayStation 6 - not yet named as such - which is currently being worked on in the company's gaming division. She noted that the console is "progressing as scheduled" and that staff are making "solid progress" on the machine (thanks, VGC). Tao also revealed that it's been a strong year for the PS5; total sales for the console have reached 97.9 million, thanks to a further 2.6 million sales throughout July, August and September 2026.

The most interesting bytes of information teased out of this call relate to Tao's claim that Sony has been able to offset the rise in memory costs via cost reductions and price increases, all helped by a yearly operating income boost of 89 percent. Sony notes that it has secured enough memory hardware for its next business year, which helps prepare the ground for PlayStation 6 production which should kick off in earnest next year.

"Although new PS5 unit sales are gradually declining as expected at this stage of the console life cycle, the PlayStation platform continues to expand and grow in a stable manner," Tao explained. "[Next year,] we intend to make solid progress in preparing for the next-generation platform."

Tao outlines that Sony is beginning to pivot towards this new platform in terms of both investment and production, and that Sony will "attach great importance to a new platform and make the necessary investments for that." This platform - the as-yet-unofficially-named PS6 - will be announced "at an appropriate time in the future".

This all follows reports that the PS6's memory and storage alone reportedly cost more than $680, and that there is still no hard release date set for the console. In light of the fact that console manufacturing is being heavily impacted by the on-going component shortage, many are expecting the price of the base PS6 to be over $1000. We will have to see what Sony announces over the next year before we know for certain.

#3856. Ahead of The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past, here's a "lore friendly unofficial expansion to Geralt's life in Toussaint" from a well-established quest modder

While its remastered upgrade might have broken cover in late September, The Witcher 3's extra expansion isn't set to join it until next year. With 2027 still a month and a bit away, a modder's taken it upon themselves to add a few more adventures to Geralt's time in Toussaint, Blood and Wine's gorgeous French-ish duchy, before the bloke from the river heads off to Letten for Songs of the Past.

So far, only the opening chapter of the mod - Annals of the Duchy - has been released. It adds in a new quest about Geralt, with help from either Yen or Triss if either have made the trip out to Toussaint as part of your playthrough, getting into a scrape thanks to a halfling who seems to promise Gerry the chance to juice up his vineyard's vines.

The mod's creator, Jontej, has previously put together a couple of other custom Witcher 3 quests. While they do look to have used AI voices in English versions of those mods, for Annals of the Duchy they've enlisted a cast of human actors for both Enlish and Polish versions.

Jontej has plans to expand this new questline going forwards, having cited specific "plans for an extra storyline involving Syanna", whom you might remember from Blood and Wine's main quest. Given that - spoilers ahead - the mod relies on you having gotten the Blood and Wine ending which sees both Anna Henrietta and Syanna survive, as well as having paid to renovate the gardens of Geralt's vineyard. They add that, when it comes to their additions, the "timeline fits quite well [with] the upcoming official Songs of the Past Expansion, which has been confirmed to take place after the events of the main game/Blood and Wine".

As much as I've argued that, as of right now, I struggle to see how Songs of the Past will manage to outdo Blood and Wine as a satisfying end to Geralt's tale in the Witcher game trilogy, I am intrigued by the idea of a few more modded adventures showing Gerry adjusting to the semi-retired life. After all, Toussaint's got to have a few more dungeons tucked away that're worth temporarily dusting off the White Wolf's twin swords for.

To kick off Annals of the Duchy, you'll need to trigger its first quest by taking a stroll from the Corvo Bianco manor house down to its gardens between 11am and 1pm. It's worth noting that any other mod which messes with Yen, Triss or companions in general has a chance to muck things up as far as Jontej's creation goes.

#3855. Extraction shooters need a PvE mode for casual players—so what’s the controversy?

This idea isn't half as controversial as half of you make it out to be.

Any major extraction shooter release inevitably summons the age-old debate of PvE vs. PvP. It’s been the case with ARC Raiders and DMZ, and that schism will resurface whenever the next one launches. You can always count on heated arguments stirring controversy about something that shouldn’t be controversial at all.

After all, how dare players enjoy PvE in a PvPvE game? The way the debate often goes, you’d assume it was a cardinal sin, like the PvE crowd was planning to personally tar and feather every PvP player in existence.

Instead, PvE players often just want a more forgiving, relaxed experience that does not involve getting ratted to death in Stella Montis or having to spend an entire match in Hajin with one’s butthole clenched so tightly that not even a Wi-Fi signal passes through it. And from the looks of it, this isn’t a small crowd, either.

Take ARC Raiders, for example. The demand for a PvE mode was so large that Embark tested a toggle that disabled damage between players last month. Before then, 37 percent of its fanbase (and growing) were focused on PvE cooperation, 34 were there purely for PvP (stable since launch), and 27 landed in the middle, Embark said. Over 51 percent of all surveyed users showed interest in a dedicated PvE mode, according to the studio.

If even the thought of discussing this makes you feel like Ben Affleck with a cigarette, you’re not the only one who’s exhausted. The PvE vs. PvP argument is the reheated leftovers from the skill-based matchmaking debate, annoyingly inescapable when battle royales were all the rage.

Often, the higher-skill players don’t want to match against others of similar ability because their games get too difficult and stop being fun. And yes, this is exactly what happens to lower-skill players without SBMM.

Activision ran a famous experiment with its matchmaking in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3 in 2024. The company loosened the skill constraints for half of its players during a month. At the end of the test, it noted that the 10 percent of affected players at the top of the skill pyramid returned more often, but the remaining 90 percent were considerably less likely to come back. And that’s with a diluted SBMM.

“If [SBMM] were completely removed, we would expect to see the player population erode rapidly in the span of a few months, resulting in a negative outcome for all our players,” the study said.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

PvP is zero-sum by definition: for one to win, another must lose. Unsurprisingly, it doesn’t feel good to be on the losing side. Having the chance to opt out of that and into a different playstyle altogether shouldn’t cause this much uproar—especially not in a game where keeping gear plays a major role. And often, it doesn’t even relate exclusively to skill, but the type of experience one wants to have.

This time, it’s not even a matter of catering to one part of the audience in detriment of another, which would be an understandable concern if it made a modicum of sense. Embark isn’t going to make your fingers fall off every time you shoot another player. Having PvE in DMZ won’t make Activision cease content for Warzone or multiplayer, otherwise CoD Zombies wouldn’t exist.

Often, the people contemplated by PvE mode aren’t even in the game, but they’re yearning to be. The lack of full-on PvE in DMZ didn’t make me flock to multiplayer; it made me uninstall the game altogether. I only bought ARC Raiders because of the PvE test and the game’s aggression-based matchmaking. If that went away, I’d disappear with it. My friends did so the second the PvE test ended, and they’re eagerly waiting for the mode to return.

Extraction shooters being unapproachable made sense when they were niche. Now that every live-service seems to flirt with the genre, though, they should be more welcoming, especially if they want to draw a larger crowd.

As an avid frequenter of friendly lobbies in ARC Raiders, I’ve had more positive experiences with randoms than I can count, and that’s a big reason why I open the game. I’m having one hell of a time fighting Matriarchs, defibbing other raiders, and dropping duplicate blueprints. My archenemy was a cat bed, and I’m thrilled this was the case. It sucks when it’s tooth-and-nail all the time, as every big opponent of SBMM will tell you.

The difference is, unlike hero shooters or battle royales, extraction shooters already have a PvE element baked into them, no retrofitting required. Of course, you may have to reshuffle some things, like increasing the difficulty of the AI-controlled enemies to raise the threat and keep players on their toes. But it’s different from creating something entirely new, like if people wanted bots in Apex Legends or full-blooded PvP in the extraction-adjacent Helldivers 2. And it’s certainly not too much to ask.

There’s a reason extraction shooters were somewhat obscure before the gaming industry threw a borderline infinite amount of money at making the genre mainstream. Soulslikes aside, not everyone wants to get their teeth kicked in as a pastime. Sure, the cutthroat uncertainty from PvPvE shaped the identity of ARC Raiders, but there are ways to evoke that without fighting other players, as Helldivers 2 and GTFO have proved.

ARC Raiders has come a long way in the past year, in no small part because of the 37 percent of PvE players (and in bigger part because of the 63 percent of other raiders). Maybe the burgeoning PvE scene changes the vision of the game somewhat, and that’s fine. DMZ getting a fully PvE mode wouldn’t be entirely out of the realm of possibility, considering that’s basically what MWZ was. That’s the beauty and bane of live services: there’s always room for reinvention.

Destructoid's former Destiny 2 expert (RIP), Pedro now spends way too much time concocting builds in Warframe, playing Elden Ring, or practicing guitar. He's been writing professionally since 2019 and takes psychic damage every time someone forgets an Oxford comma.

World of Warcraft: Forever is fascinating from so many perspectives—not necessarily in terms of what's on offer (it is, despite my enamorment, still very much Classic WoW) but in what it means for the MMO genre at large.

It's the kind of project that usually only gets cooked up in "what ifs", a version of a 20-year old game that decided not to go for expansions, but to instead spread out horizontally. A World of Warcraft that didn't have to rush a single hour of development time. It's an attempt at not only just recreating nostalgia, but applying a fine layer of polish to that nostalgia.

Forever has over 1,000 new quests and dungeons—and having played some of them in my 50 hours with its beta, I can say that Blizzard has absolutely nailed what I've seen so far. To restore a prior version of a game is one thing, but to add new areas and content that feel appropriate to its old school game design feels like a magic trick.

It's like someone's dusted off a set of forbidden texts and started reading them in flawless ancient Greek—a sleight-of-hand that's been dunked on as a "millennial retirement home" but, as the exact target audience for Forever, I've gotta say: Bingo night's really popping.

Let's start with the dungeons. I went through the new romp, Ruins of Lordaeron, and was clocked sideways with a feeling of familiarity, despite it being the first time I'd ever set foot there—modern MMO dungeons are like theme park rides, where you strap yourself in and get funnelled through a series of hallways to knock over bosses for fat loot and a ton of quest XP.

And listen, I love rollercoasters. But I had no idea how much I'd missed that slower, more ponderous pace. Having to manually ask for invites, spending a half-hour collecting quests outside of the dungeon itself, journeying there on foot, and then once you're in—carefully pulling group after group in a sprawling maze where you can legitimately get lost.

It ruled. It still rules, that's what surprised me—there's merit to this older way of doing things that transcends the rose-tinted glasses I'm wary of, and it's not even because the game's harder. Quite the contrary: Doing solid DPS as a level 18 warrior is pretty easy, I just hit Heroic Strike every now and then and try not to rip aggro too much.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

But the lo-fi pace of it all, even if it does take longer, is downright lovely. It has a quality all of its own—one that's so refreshing in a world of seasonal grinds. And that expands to the questing, too.

I've talked about the classic pace of questing on the site before, but the light touch Blizzard has applied here is marvellous—the original WoW was riddled with huge gaps in questing zones that were either unfinished or simply barren when it came to questlines, even though its intention back in 2004 was to avoid that. Many of these places—and new questing zones entirely—are getting added with Forever.

I didn't have a direct template to compare it to, but I felt it: Forever paves over these yawning gaps in the questing experience, but it doesn't modernise questing itself. They're still put in inconvenient areas, they're still given to you in massive batches, and they're still sometimes a massive pain in the butt.

But layering new stuff on top of that old chassis means the engine runs smoother. The satisfaction of a long, multi-hour journey across a zone pairs so sweetly with the dopamine hit of turning all your quests in at once. A hit that I just don't really get in modern theme park MMOs anymore.

Sometimes I had to travel to different zones because I was being outlevelled by quests, sure, but I was never stuck, I never had to grind. And if Blizzard can keep that tempo going for the rest of its 30 levels, I'm going to be wrapped up in a cozy loop of old school questing for the foreseeable future.

You can check out WoW: Forever via the BattleNet launcher on the game's official website.

#3853. World of Warcraft: Forever is off to a great start with Blizzard's smoothest launch in memory

World of Warcraft: Forever came out last night. Those who stayed up were prepared for the usual from major WoW releases: long queues, disconnects, and server lag. However, save for a few minor hiccups here and there, things went off without a hitch.

Eurogamer can report first-hand that for European players who stayed up from, let's say 11pm - 3:50am last night, the login queues were short and constantly moving. Those who were very keen to get in the moment servers went live ran into unclickable server selection boxes, but backing out and re-joining the short queue fixed this problem swiftly.

Once you got in, there was very little server lag save for a lost spell cast or two, nor were constant random disconnects that would boot you out into the cold (I didn't get disconnected once - a record). As far as WoW launches go, an incredibly smooth first day.

This was acknowledged by World of Warcraft developers, such as executive producer Holly Longdale who wrote on X: "At the risk of jinxing things, so far so goodish which is crazy by itself. The team prepared a lot since the wildness of Beta. And this launch was crazier than the insanity we imagined but thankfully the team built plans and contingencies. They are incredible in my opinion.".

Josh "Aggrend" Greenfield, a senior game designer on World of Warcraft Forever, addressed some minor issues that did pop up. These include a zone population problem: in basic terms the megaservers split players into different shards, and some of these felt a bit empty of players. There was also a quirk with the various big boats and zeppelins dotted around the map, which were busted. Temporary portals were added to provide a workaround.

"Thanks for everyone making this a great, super smooth launch," Greenfield wrote. "I’m going to head home and 'go to sleep' now. Yep, sleeping. Totally not playing WoW Forever until 3am. Nope."

The reaction to this silky smooth launch has some players flabbergasted. "I can't believe how smooth this launch is" is the title of Reddit user Arizhela's post, currently topping the WoW Forever board. They continue: "I fully expected to not be able to play today, but I logged in with no queue and no lag."

Another post, created in the early hours of this morning, is dubbed: "Never take a day off for launch, they said" in which a WoW player regrets not booking some time off from work this week, expecting problems. "You've been finessed son," replied user SnooWalruses3948, while SirePuns shared in the shock: "The advice was sound, but this time around the developers hired a witch I tell you. The code must’ve been witchcraft, the hardware must’ve been blessed by a witch as well."

It is unclear just how well World of Warcraft: Forever's launch was, given the unsocialable and employment-averse release time in the dead of night for us Europeans, but it follows a record-breaking beta period in which many hopped back into the MMO. Impressions from this beta were largely positive, the magic of the old MMO seemingly recaptured.
