#3820. "Is there any accountability left in this world?" Warren Spector pops off at EA executives and their massive payouts as BioWare shuts down

It's only been two weeks since we last heard Warren Spector sound off about EA's sudden decision to close BioWare, following the publisher's acquisition by Saudi Arabia's PIF and venture capitalist concerns. But now, the storied developer is back and - apparently - angrier than ever.

"I recently posted my thoughts about EA’s shuttering of BioWare," Spector wrote in a post on LinkedIn. "Those of you who read my post know that I was unhappy. I remain so. The tragedy of so many layoffs the last few years hasn’t been lost on me, but for some reason, BioWare hit me on an emotional level that nothing before had. I felt gut-punched."

Spector goes on to counter the idea that the studio was closed down as a "sound business decision" because the "studio’s glory days (artistic and commercial) were behind them" and that "businesses don’t succeed on history alone". These reactions, more than anything else, appear to be what's inspired Spector to take to posting again - he simply cannot agree with this assessment.

"If studio-level people leave, resulting in dilution of talent, someone is creating an environment that pushes them out. Do those culture-killers pay any price? If executives misread the market, over-hire, or make decisions that result in under-funded, over-funded, poorly-marketed games do they lose sleep let alone jobs?" he asks.

"Do those same executives suffer like developers when the needs of financial partners and private investors take precedence over the people who actually create value, let alone over the interests of players? Does anyone up there in or adjacent to the C-suite care? Is there any accountability left in this world? Obviously not."

He then goes on to list the yearly payouts that some of the highest-level executives at EA are rewarded per annum. These include:

"Tens of thousands of do-ers and makers are out of work and these people think they're worth that kind of compensation?" continues Spector. "And if you think this is a discussion about 'sound business decisions', I hope you never get anywhere near running a business. Or at least that people have the sense not to go work for you."

Back in August, we saw Warren Spector announce his intention to retire from the world of video game development. Spector's announcement comes shortly after the last game he worked on - Thick as Thieves - had its final major update only a few months after its release. Despite its charm and low price, Thick as Thieves sadly didn't sell what it needed to, resulting in layoffs at Spector's studio.

This all comes as the US takes an increasingly hawkish stance toward China, framing AI development as a national security issue and restricting the sale of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies. Meanwhile, US-based AI companies and their aggressive datacenter buildouts are proving increasingly unpopular with American voters.

#3817. Former Rockstar Games tech director thinks GTA 6 could be coming to PC sooner than you'd expect to curb AI clones

Former Rockstar Games North technical director Obbe Vermeij believes that the possibility of AI vibe coded ports of Grand Theft Auto 6 could push Rockstar to create an official PC version sooner than you'd expect.

Speaking to RockPaperShotgun as part of a wider interview, Vermeij said generative AI "really has changed the world.". He elaborated: "I think I would be concerned, if I was Rockstar, that somebody would just take the PS5 version and get AI to change it to PC, which won't be as good as [the developer's] effort, but it could still also hurt their sales. So, I wouldn't be surprised if there was an effort to get [the releases] a little bit closer together."

Vermeij emphasised that he doesn't know what Rockstar's plans are, but with his technical expertise, he does believe that generative AI tools are "probably" capable of pulling off a GTA 6 PC port.

"It will take a long time. It actually, physically takes hours and hours and hours to do these things," Vermeij said. "And it will take a bunch of tokens and everything, so it would probably cost like, tens of thousands of dollars in tokens. But like, you know, if it's GTA, I think people are gonna try it.".

We've already seen people thrust footage of Grand Theft Auto 6 into AI software over the past few months. AI slop videos have been pulling in millions of views on social media, and people have been 'improving' trailer footage with Nvidia's DLSS5 'yassification' machine (thanks Ars Technica). Grand Theft Auto 6 itself will not feature any generative AI or microtransactions at launch.

AI game clones continue to be a problem. Game developers have cancelled public demos in fear of having their game copied, and Steam owner Valve has gone out to say it's the developer's responsibility to prevent cloning by making their games more original. Even as Anthropic has introduced measures to prevent such practices, other AI software can still perform such tasks.

#3815. Return Of The Living Dead Cast Horrified By AI-Made Sequel They Were Originally Set To Star In

Last weekend was Halloween. A night for creeps. An evening of shrieks. For some scream queen royalty, they got one of the more unpleasant kinds of frights. Richard Driscoll, who crowdfunded a sequel to the 1985 punk zombie classic Return of the Living Dead, published the new film on his website. This came to the surprise to the original cast, who were attached to star in the follow-up. Instead it seems Driscoll opted to use AI to generate the film, leaving fans and alumni more aghast at him than the flesh eating ghouls.

“This is not what we signed up for,” says Beverly Randolph on the Caffeinated Horror Dude podcast. “We got to get something out there because there’s so much hate on us right now.”

Due to some erroneous paperwork, George A. Romeroâs original Night of the Living Dead was released directly into the public domain in 1968. Because of this, it enabled any director and studio, including Romero himself, to develop âsequelsâ to the series regardless of legal claim. One of the more adored successors is Return of the Living Dead, where a gang of punk teenagers take refuge in a morgue after a melting brain eater escapes containment. It has since stood on its own as a cult classic, generating its own sequels. This includes Brian Yuznaâs grotesque Return of the Living Dead 3, which I mostly bring up because it scared the shit out of me as a kid.

In 2024, Driscoll, who operates his own no-budget streaming service “DragonFLIX,” launched an Indiegogo page for “TRASH’s REVENGE Return of the Living Dead Universe.” Unlike other fan projects, this one had a large portion of the original cast involved, with stars Randolph and Linnea Quigley acting as producers. It also threw in Quigleyâs fellow Sorority Babe in the Slimeball Bowl-O-Rama Michelle Bauer and the Oscar nominated Eric Roberts, who has seemingly been in everything except The Living Dead.

From what Quigley described, this movie was intended to be a blend of Sunset Boulevard and Rocky Horror. Trash, Quigleyâs character who was last seen as a nudist zombie, had become a Norma Desmond recluse, relishing in the glory days of her brain eating spree. This sounds incredible. But after some confusion and radio silence between the cast and director, this incredible movie did not come to be.

Last Halloween night, Driscoll pushed out The Return of the Living Dead: Aftermath, an almost entirely AI generated heap of rotting flesh. The results wonât surprise you. Robotic line delivery. Nonsensical sequence of events. Object impermanence. Everythingâs wet. Everyone looks shocked. At one point the video just flips around like youâre watching on a phone someone dropped. And while the Return cast didnât film any of this footage, their likenesses are peppered throughout.

James Gunn says "the characters we set up will live on" as he departs as the co-CEO of DC Studios

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

James Gunn has released a separate, lengthy statement amid the news that he and co-CEO Peter Safran are no longer the heads of DC Studios.

"There have been so many highs along the way: releasing Superman and Clayface, making Peacemaker, reading the scripts to The People Vs., the entire process of Man of Tomorrow, which thus far has been the best filmmaking experience of my life, and numerous other moments," Gunn wrote on his personal Instagram account.

Gunn also lamented that he "disliked the at-times corporate nature of the job" and had the "most difficulty" with "dividing my time between projects I’m incredibly passionate about and the ones I’m not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head."

"So, yes, I will miss the people around me, and I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I'm also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking. That's not to say Peter and I are immediately done with DC or superheroes. We have Man of Tomorrow out this summer. And we've just been engaged on another DC project which I'm writing, and we'll see where it goes after that. And of course, the characters we set up will live on." You can read the full statement below.

The statement comes amid the shocking news that Gunn and Safran would be replaced by former Marvel Studios executive Jeremy Latcham, effective December 1. The duo was first appointed to the position back in 2022, having released three movies: Superman, Supergirl, and Clayface, and four TV shows: Creature Commandos, Peacemaker season 2, The Penguin, and Lanterns, over the last four years. Still to come are Man of Tomorrow, The People V Gorilla Grodd, Creature Commandos season 2, and the long-awaited The Batman: Part II.

Of course, this change is no doubt part of the Skydance merger, which sees Paramount in full control of Warner Bros. and everything Warner Bros. owns. It's worth noting that, before Gunn and Safran were appointed, Warner Bros. executives reportedly wanted an overhaul of DC in favor of putting classic heroes back at the forefront and making them a bit less dark/more kid-friendly. That said, it's possible that Skydance executives want fewer projects like The People v. Gorilla Grodd and Creature Commandos, and more big-hitters on screen, like Wonder Woman or Aquaman... and finally Batman (who still only exists as part of Matt Reeves' Elseworlds; the DCU has yet to cast a Batman). It also probably doesn't help that Supergirl was a massive critical and commercial failure.

Man of Tomorrow hits theaters on July 9, 2027. For more, here are all the upcoming DC movies and shows announced before Gunn's departure.

#3813. Following BioWare's shock closure, a new documentary capturing its final moments is coming next year

A documentary detailing the history of beloved Mass Effect studio BioWare is releasing next year, and will cover last month's shock closure of the studio, following the private acquisition of owner EA.

Mass Effect: The BioWare Story (per Deadline) has been written and directed by Akash Sherman and produced for Canada's Super Channel. It documents the studio from the early days after its founding in 1995 to the release of barn-burner hits like Mass Effect and Dragon Age. Filming began two years prior to the announcement of BioWare's closure and continued throughout, with Deadline reporting the documentary will "capture BioWare’s final chapter."

The BioWare Story includes interviews with studio founders Ray Muzyka, Greg Zeschuk, and Augustine Yip, alongside Mass Effect director Casey Hudson, other BioWare developers, and Shepard voice actor Jennifer Hale. That's alongside former EA CEO John Riccitiello, LucasFilm Games vice president Douglas Reilly, and creator of The Game Awards Geoff Keighley.

"The BioWare founders are my hometown heroes,” writer and director Sherman said in a statement accompanying the documentary news. "It's a privilege and responsibility to share the journey of underdogs who came together to create deeply beloved storytelling. Their golden era kindled a spark in me and in an entire generation. With the studio's recent closure, the film is now a profound valediction."

For fans outside Canada, Mass Effect: The BioWare Story is planned for a major film festival run and a world premiere next year. No exact release date has been established as of writing.

Members of the games industry have lambasted EA's decision to close Bioware in the weeks since the news was shared, with legendary designer Warren Spector writing, "Anyone who participated in this travesty should be ashamed". Meanwhile, a petition has reached enough signatures for the Canadian government to potentially rescue the studio from closure. Whether or not it actually does… Well, weirder things have happened?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On a recent visit to Jackbox Games HQ here in Chicago, I got to speak with developers and studio leadership about their process, history, and place in the industry. Given, you know, everything, I'm pretty much contractually obligated to ask about AI in conversations like this. Here's what CEO Mike Bilder had to say on the topic:

"The people are what make this product. The comedy, the writing, and the art, all that is done by people, and we have no intention of changing that. I don't think we're experts on what's going on with AI in the industry and any of that. There's obviously uses for tooling and for research, and [for] all that kind of stuff [AI is] incredibly powerful.

"But from a generative asset standpoint, we don't have any intention of replacing people, or people-made editorial and art with it."

From everything we had discussed up to this point, as well as Jackbox's whole deal, I didn't think generative AI would really be in the cards for the studio. But I still appreciated Bilder's straightforward, clear answer on the subject, particularly when the standard playbook these days is fence sitting reminiscent of The Simpsons' "Abortions for some, miniature American flags for others."

Jackbox's games are relatively lightweight from a tech perspective, while the art and writing is their main draw⁠—if anything was noticeably AI-generated, it would put the value of the whole package into question.

The company recently released the Jackbox Party Pack 12 on October 14, and the studio's production values have really progressed since the last entry I had played⁠—Trivia Murder Party 3 makes extensive use of realtime 3D graphics, for example. Jackbox Party Pack 12 is available on pretty much everything, but this is Personal Computer Gamer, so I'll say you can grab it on Steam.

#3809. Marvel Rivals season 11 countdown: Exact start time and date

Marvel Rivals’ next big season is nearly here, and after things slowed down a bit in season 10 with only one new playable character, the arrival of season 11 feels especially exciting. If you’re looking forward to this one, you’ll want to know exactly when season 11 is launching.

Although Marvel Rivals sees minor updates weekly, it’s the big seasonal updates like this one where the real changes and additions occur. There’s lots to look forward to as always, so to make sure you’re ready to dive in, here’s the exact time and date when season 11 of Marvel Rivals begins.

Season 11 of Marvel Rivals arrives on Nov. 13. We don’t have a precise launch time, and we likely won’t get one ahead of release. Despite this, the game sticks to a very reliable and consistent release schedule, which means there’s an unofficial but generally very dependable timeframe for the update maintenance and release.

As long as everything stays on track and sticks to the same schedule as usual, season 11 should go live at 5am CT. Maintenance should start around 9am UTC, and after about two hours of downtime, servers should be back up so you can start playing.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

Marvel Rivals season 11 will be approximately one month long. This is about how long all seasons are. Halfway through this period, the game will see another big update and a transition into season 11.5.

As of the time of writing, the season 11 heroes have not been officially revealed. However, we do have some key clues that may hint at who’s to come in the final Gallery Card for season 10.5. Every season, the final card provides clues for what’s to come next, so it’s a fairly reliable way to predict the featured characters coming soon.

The first character who seems to be teased for season 11 is Nightcrawler. In the Gallery Card, Moon Girl is holding his sword. Since this clue is the boldest, he’ll likely be our launch hero.

The second character isn’t quite as clear, but based on all of the Doomsday tie-in events, the name of the Gallery Card, which is “Doomsday is near,” and the details of the story featured with this card, it might be Doctor Doom himself. If not, there’s also a mysterious bat symbol featured prominently in this art, which could point to someone like Dracula, or perhaps Green Goblin.

Season 11 of Marvel Rivals will add new content to just about every area of the game, as is the case with all seasonal updates. Here’s a breakdown of all features we know are included in this update.

Before season 11 arrives, it’s a good idea to check off all the current events in season 10.5, as not all of them will be sticking around. Make sure you fully complete all Night of Illusions puzzles, jump into Avengers: Endgame, and test out Avengers: Infinity War.

#3808. Square Enix accidentally botches a Nier: Automata update, balloons required file size from 50GB to 366GB on PC

"Do you think games are silly little things?"

Yesterday, Nier: Automata received a new patch on Steam, adding more language support to the title - it can now be played with Korean, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese options - but this new update also, somehow, inflated the file size of the game on PC from about 50GB to 366GB. D'oh! What's worse is, the update is not optional.

The cause of this, reportedly, is a bug that caused all the DLC in the YoRHa Edition of the game to become the same size as the base game - and the new download stacks them all concurrently. "Only SquareEnix can turn 40GB into 366GB with 8GB patch," says one dissatisfied Steam reviewer.

If you don't have space for this massive new file on your PC (and I can't say I blame you, it's ridiculous), there is a workaround, as confirmed by Square Enix in a tweet via its Japanese Twitter account.

"We have confirmed an issue where, following the latest update to the Steam version of Nier: Automata, the installation process indicates that more storage space is required than expected," noted the publisher. "We are currently investigating the cause and working on a solution. We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. As a temporary workaround, you can download the base game by unchecking the DLC under Steam → Properties → DLC."

It's quite ironic, really, that so many Steam reviewers are complaining about things like "I just need to delete 90% of my computer to install this" when a large part of the game is managing the software/programmes installed on your android protagonists in order to upgrade your abilities and stats. There's even an ending for uninstalling your OS on your mechanical main characters. I'd be inclined to suggest this is some sort of meta psy-op from creator Yoko Taro, but… nah, that's just fantasy, isn't it? Isn't it?

Speaking of Taro, earlier this year we learned that "Nier Automata will continue", though we only heard back in 2025 that most of the projects the developer was working on were cancelled. One of these may have been the Tencent-backed Nier mobile game in 2024, which reportedly "struggled to find a monetisation to offset its high costs."

It's only been a couple of months that we've known about the existence of Diablo 5, and as such there are a ton of open questions about the direction it'll take. Blizzard teased a few fundamentals during BlizzCon 2026, like the fact that it'll take place in a Sanctuary that's been completely overtaken by Diablo and his minions, and that there will no longer be any traditional towns or safe havens to hide from the bad guys. It's been clear to me that Blizzard is doubling down on the horror-driven bleakness that defined the first game in the series, and there are blatant call-backs to the series' roots in the itemization and procedurally generated environments, but there's still a lot left unanswered about what it'll be like to actually play Diablo 5.

Chris Wilson, co-creator of Path of Exile and noted Diablo 2 mega fan, has been encouraged by everything Blizzard has shown of Diablo 5, but has one concern based on the messaging so far. Referencing comments from Diablo leadership at this year's BlizzCon suggesting Blizzard is surveying all generations of players from Diablo 1 to 4, Wilson says he's worried Blizzard might be trying to appeal to too many different audiences at once. He points out that Blizzard didn't even label Diablo an action-RPG series until Diablo 2: Lord of Destruction, and that Diablo 3 and 4 each appeal to a different type of player as well.

"This means that when you survey Diablo players and say 'what would you like in a Diablo 5, how can we get you to play it?', you're gonna get many different answers, and I worry that some of these answers might be slightly mutually exclusive," Wilson says in an interview with Destin Legarie. "I'm optimistic by what they showed because there's heavy Diablo 2 signaling, and that's really cool. I just would urge caution, of, it's OK to not appeal to every Diablo player as long as the product that's made is really fun for the core audience you're targeting, and I'm sure they are thinking of the core audience. Like, I'm simplifying it a lot here, but that's my one worry, really, that they go a bit too broad.

"There's a saying, if you make a game for everyone, you make a game for no one," Wilson concludes.

I understand where Wilson's coming from as a fellow Diablo 1+2 diehard, but it seems a little premature to be worrying about a too-safe Diablo 5 based on such limited information. There are all sorts of reasons a developer might survey fans of a series from different entry points, and regardless of Blizzard's reasoning, everything we've seen so far points to the darkest Diablo yet, which if anything stands in stark contrast to a game like Diablo 3. Meanwhile, the aforementioned return to procedural generation and Diablo 2-style itemization further suggests an embrace of the series' roots rather than some broad-strokes appeal to every generation of Diablo player.

This could very well be pure hopium, but the overall vibe I'm getting as a lifelong Diablo player, and as someone who attended this year's BlizzCon and spoken directly with Blizzard, is that the original Diablo is at the forefront of the studio's mind as it works on Diablo 5. To be very, very clear, that's just the collective impression that's formed in my head over dozens of interviews, panels, and videos scanned, and not something I was explicitly told by Blizzard, but it's exactly what I'm hoping for nonetheless.

Diablo 4's nostalgic new season has convinced me that we need a Diablo 1 remake more than Diablo 5

Though it didn't have a specific release date, Slitherine's refresh of the Warhammer-themed fantasy football game was scheduled for a full release in 2026. As of the announcement made at the Dominion Days showcase in Berlin, that's no longer the case.

"The game's history and the feedback received during the latest playtest have reinforced the team's belief that the game needs to be as polished as possible," Slitherine said, "as disappointing the fans is not an option."

That playtest is ongoing, and has just added an Arena mode where you try to make it through 10 matches in a row without losing a game or being forced to a draw more than twice. It's played in resurrection format, which means your team returns to its starting lineup at the end of each match, with no improvements or losses to carry over, so you better make sure your roster's a strong one from the off.

Slitherine also confirmed that Warhammer Blood Bowl's two new factions, the Tomb Kings and Bretonnians, will be added to the base game for free. Everyone who owns Blood Bowl 3 will be upgraded to Warhammer Blood Bowl without cost, and will get to keep access to any teams and cosmetics they've already paid for.

#3805. I regret talking crap about the Ocarina of Time Remake

The Ocarina of Time remake is out, and we might have an all-timer on our hands. I never doubted Nintendo’s commitment to one of its greatest titles, but I was never sold on its looks, so I made my voice heard. Next time, I’ll let them cook.

I wrote a piece about the Internet’s reception to the Ocarina of Time Remake‘s aesthetics. Lots of people online immediately vibed with what they saw, but a bunch of people were having none of it. It’s even possible that the haters were in the minority, but this is the Internet, and Twitter especially, so negativity will always get the spotlight.

The piece also featured my opinion, and I, despite being pretty much more ok with it than most of the detractors, still wasn’t very keen on the looks. I felt like the game featured an unbecoming mix between fantastical and realistic graphics that I just couldn’t shake. I still don’t love the looks, but I have since learned something very important by looking at the people’s reaction to the actual game.

People are absolutely gushing over it, and it’s not a case of people simply getting their yearly dose of nostalgia. Players, new and old alike, are engaging with it as if it’s this bold new thing that either reignites or creates a completely newfound appreciation for games. That’s the best a game can ever do, both for the player and the industry as a whole.

Though I’ve witnessed accounts of people who’d gotten estranged from games talking about getting pulled back in just because it’s OoT, this is not just a game; this is a very powerful event capable of going from reuniting players with their younger selves to connecting kids with the parents who grew up with the original.

Take a look at the original OoT‘s graphics. They’re far below today’s standard, and since it’s time for me to confess and atone, let me add that I was never too crazy about its colors, which always felt too desaturated for me. I only played it for the first time when I got my GameCube back in ’03 with the famous Wind Waker + OoT bundle and, guess what, as soon as I jumped in, I stopped caring about the graphics altogether.

Graphics are a great selling point, but they’re not what keeps players engaged until the end, especially in an action-adventure title. It’s always going to be the gameplay, and that’s why gamers love higher framerates. Studios might prefer games to look better at the cost of it, because even though the game’s feel while playing dictates how it imprints in your heart and memory, it’s the screenshots that do most of the selling. Sadly, those never show how the game runs and plays.

I have had a bone to pick with remakes for the longest time. Though I believe the first Resident Evil remake, one of the first of its kind, remains one of the finest games of all time, it has mostly just been downhill in the diminishing returns lane since then. I think the best example of what I’m talking about is that of the Resident Evil 4 remake, which adds a neat layer of shiny new paint to one of the greatest games of all time, but forgets most of the superb direction choices that made people fall in love with it for the first time.

At its worst, the Ocarina of Time remake is the exact opposite. It’s a game with graphics that some won’t like, but with a heart so powerful it won’t just make players remember how cool it was to play the original; it will make them feel the kind of childlike wonder they thought they would never encounter again. Or, in short, it’s making us all feel like the Nintendo 64 kid.

Ever been as happy to be gifted a console as that kid? Maybe, if you got a console right about when he did, when 3D games completely shattered our image of what games could be, and the amount of fun they could bring. If you’re a gamer, that was, for a long time, the video that came to mind when you thought about heartwarming vids, because many of us are fortunate to know exactly what that feels like. That’s not the kind of reaction a kid makes simply for being fed the seeds of consumerism; that’s an earnest reaction to encountering a portal to 388 awesome new worlds, or 387, because one of them is Superman 64‘s.

By trashing or amplifying the voices of those talking crap about Ocarina of Time’s new coming before it’s even out, I risked driving people away from ever becoming that kid again, and that’s the worst thing a gamer can legally do. So, if you have the chance to try out Ocarina of Time’s Remake, do it—even if you don’t immediately vibe with its looks.

Tiago is a freelancer who used to write about video games, cults, and video game cults. He now writes for Destructoid in an attempt to find himself on the winning side when the robot uprising comes.

#3804. World of Warcraft: Forever hotfix puts a stop to super speedy flag carriers that were dominating PvP battlegrounds

World of Warcraft: Forever has received its first major hotfix patch, which among other things has put an end to an especially powerful bug that made PvP battlegrounds like Warsong Gulch favoured to the Horde's advantage.

While Taurens are running, they gradually build up stacks of increased movement speed. They gain a two percent movement speed bonus per stack, and it stacks up to 30 times. That means a Tauren can gain 60 percent increased movement speed, though it's worth noting that when they stop moving, these stacks decrease. In short, cows run fast.

The Hotfix, detailed in this Blizzard blog post, stops the Tauren's plainsrunning passive from stacking during a battleground's preparation phase. What players were doing to exploit this was running back and forth in the minutes before the Warsong Gulch battleground let both teams loose. It's a capture the flag game mode, so once the gates opened, Taurens were sprinting ahead of everyone else, allowing them to quickly push towards the enemy base for a potential early flag capture.

In addition, the hotfix removes any plainsrunning stacks from Taurens once they pick up the enemy flag, and prevents them from gaining stacks while the flag is in their possession. The goal of the enemy team is to stop and kill the enemy flag carrier as soon as possible, so a Tauren moving far faster than any of your team made this pretty difficult.

Tauren's could be tanky warriors or druids too, which further added to the difficulty in killing them. With this change they're now easier to lock down, though it's worth noting a Tauren can still make use of Plainsrunning to rush into the enemy base early. They just don't have that wild speed boost from the jump.

Surely this was the only reason my Alliance Warsong Gulch games were all lost this morning, and not because my faction is for chumps. In other World of Warcraft: Forever news, the launch earlier this week was applauded as one of the smoothest in the series history, save for a few broken boats and zeppelins.

The hotfix has also decreased the respawn time of the NPC Deathstalker Erland who is needed for an escort quest. People were mulling around his spawn and wasting away while waiting for him to respawn. Also, supply vendors on the Zephras Isle have been stocked with handy tradeskill bags that you could find in other starter zones. It's the shipping I assume, it takes a while for stock to make it all the way up there.

Hollow Knight: Silksong has a new physical edition, and early arrivals reveal a surprise message from developer Team Cherry regarding additional content coming to the game in the months and, seemingly, years ahead.

Metroidvania marketing man Matthew Griffin reminds fans that "Hollow Knight: Silksong (Standard Edition) is arriving soon on November 10th." It comes with a user manual, a hand-drawn map, and reversible cover art. We're most interested in that user manual, which ends with a section on "Content Packs," per images shared online by fans who got their physical copy a smidge early.

"The world of Hollow Knight: Silksong will expand with free content packs," this page of the manual reads. "Prepare for even more adventures filled with new friends, new abilities, and new ferocious foes!"

The plurality of this promise is what's raised some eyebrows. After the many DLCs Hollow Knight received, there was little doubt that Team Cherry would add a truckload of content to Silksong. This is not a studio known for restraint. But how would all those ideas be expressed? Official word of several "free content packs" containing multiple "new abilities" for protagonist Hornet has predictably excited fans.

The manual continues: "In the first giant expansion, voyage across and beneath a salt-stricken ocean brimming with mystery and menace." Here again, fans linger on this being the first giant expansion for Silksong.

Hollow Knight also got multiple DLC packs – Hidden Dreams, The Grimm Troupe, Lifeblood, and Godmaster – adding bosses, items, areas, storylines, and exacting arena challenges. Previous comments from developers Ari Gibson and William Pellen suggested Silksong may receive a similar variety of additional content, with Sea of Sorrow expected to be a Grimm Troupe-like shotgun blast of experiences.

The manual concludes with a Hollow Knight: Silksong - Sea of Sorrow emblem that reads, "Coming soon." You'll note that this, like everything else Team Cherry has said, doesn't say when soon is.

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

Last year, Team Cherry announced Sea of Sorrow and charted a 2026 launch. Apart from a February update on a port for the original Hollow Knight and a March post confirming expanded Silksong language support, the studio hasn't said anything else on its blog or social feeds all year. Pellen previously said Team Cherry would be more communicative, and we can see how that panned out. Three blog posts in a year, dare we dream?

In a read that's only slightly generous, it's possible that this blank phrasing, used in place of a definitive release date, is just generalist wording or an artifact of this physical edition's production. Maybe Team Cherry didn't want to announce anything major in such a limited product. But this does read like a step back from the 2026 target in the expansion's reveal trailer.

Team Cherry is quiet and spontaneous enough that a Sea of Sorrow shadow drop, or at least a release date with very little notice, wouldn't surprise me. Silksong's launch also came out of nowhere, giving countless other games just two weeks to flee the blast radius. But 2026 is rapidly coming to a close and we haven't heard a peep from Team Cherry about the expansion, so I also wouldn't be surprised if this manual does, as players fear, herald a delay into 2027.

Recent YouTube comments on Sea of Sorrow's trailer tell the whole story. "Team Cherry...? Where are you...?" wonders one viewer.

The vibes are very similar to those around The Duskbloods, a Nintendo Switch 2-exclusive FromSoftware game long said to be releasing in 2026. As the months flew by without any official word, a delay seemed more and more likely, though FromSoftware also notably had some negative test feedback to respond to. Lo and behold, The Duskbloods was delayed. But much like FromSoftware, Team Cherry can pretty much do what it wants, when it wants, and millions of fans will show up anyway.

#3802. Bringing Bloodborne back is tricky because "there's a lot of involved rights associated," according to former PlayStation boss

Every year, Bloodborne fans pray for the birth of another game set in FromSoftware's Lovecraftian world. Every year, we're no closer to a Bloodborne 2 or even a Bloodborne Remastered. But why? PlayStation's former head honcho, Shawn Layden, blames it on the tricky situation of rights ownership.

Asked about the noticeable lack of Bloodborne in the decade since its blood moon shone down on us all, in an interview with The Trophy Room podcast, Layden explained that returning to any beloved game is tough.

"Bringing back old games has a certain challenge to it," he said. "Can you do something that is not only respectful of the original, but can you, you know, recreate the phenomenon as it were?"

Bloodborne's situation is slightly more complicated, though. It seems that the rights are somehow split between original publisher PlayStation, developer FromSoftware and the studio's primary stakeholder Kadokawa Corporation.

"There's a lot of involved rights associated with it, and in something like that - where Sony's in there and [FromSoftware] is in there and From's parent company is in there - I think just getting everyone to sign off on the same thing is probably the biggest challenge there," Layden said.

Having led the PlayStation brand during most of its PS4 golden years, Layden said working with FromSoftware on Bloodborne and the original Demon's Souls was "fantastic."

Despite endless calls for a comeback and very stable sales more than a decade on, Bloodborne itself is still stuck on the PS4 - though it's still playable via backward compatibility on the PS5, I should add. The closest we seemingly got to a Bloodborne comeback came from Bluepoint Games, which reportedly pitched a remake sometime before parent company PlayStation shut down the acclaimed studio, though FromSoftware supposedly didn't want the project to go ahead.

Another former PlayStation executive, Shuhei Yoshida, previously speculated that Bloodborne hasn't been remade because game director and soulslike pioneer, Hidetaka Miyazaki, would prefer to handle it himself: "Miyazaki-san really, really loved Bloodborne, what he created… So I think he is interested but he's so successful and he's so busy, so he cannot do it himself, and he doesn't want anyone else to touch it."

Elsewhere, a Bloodborne animated feature is in the works with YouTuber JackSepticEye attached as a co-producer.

Maybe laying off people who know what they're doing is bad, actually.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I don't know about you, but I'm not a huge fan of the way YouTube encourages everything becoming a video that's over an hour long and doesn't have a text version available. There's a recent video putting the original Pool of Radiance into the greater context of the history of CRPGs that's almost 10 hours long, and the odds of me watching more than 10% of it are perishingly low.

Fortunately for you, we're here to convert video to text for your edification, as with The Examined Game's comprehensive interview with Skyrim lead designer Bruce Nesmith. Asked how a game as successful as Skyrim came to be, Nesmith emphasized the importance of keeping the team together.

If I had an actual blueprint on how to do it, I would be one rich son of a bitch. A lot of it comes down to we had the same team that had worked on Oblivion. The studio had not really changed dramatically. So we were able to deal with institutional knowledge at a high level that had been retained, which allows us to not make mistakes and build on successes. That was definitely key to it.

I think also we gave a high priority to making sure that the world was full. There was nowhere that you went where there wasn't at least something fun to see if not something fun to do. And it and it can be just little things, it can be a little vignette on the side of the road. It doesn't have to be a huge big adventure, but the visual storytelling was fantastic.

I go back to that sense of freedom once again, but we accelerated that in Skyrim compared to Oblivion. It makes the world feel rich when there's a variety of experiences. The same experience over and over and over again doesn't cut it. So you have a wealth of enemy types, you've got a lot of different treasure types and loot types, you're allowed to pick everything up in the world.

I have to disagree with Nesmith on the characters, because memorable NPCs are one of Skyrim's weak spots—all those people with recycled voices and limited dialogue. But he's right that Skyrim feels full despite the absence of Ubisoft-style repeatable activities. At no point do you pick up a butterfly and get a notification that says "1/100 butterflies collected". The butterflies are just there, and you can grab them and turn them into potion ingredients if you want. Then while you're out harvesting ingredients you meet a thief or a dying orc or an NPC who points you to a sidequest, and you're off on a new journey. That's what Skyrim does well.

Nesmith goes on to say depth like that was made possible, "by having people who knew what they were doing and could hit the ground running. You didn't have to train people what it meant to make an Elder Scrolls game." Instead of laying off half the Oblivion team the moment it shipped, Bethesda kept them together. "If you look at the history of AAA studios that do sequels, you'll see that repeated," Nesmith continues. "You'll see the best game in a sequence frequently was able to maintain a particular percentage of the staff—was able to maintain a vision."

#3798. Mass Effect-like RPG The Expanse: Osiris Reborn ropes in David Gaider, the original lead writer of Bioware's Dragon Age series

"Focusing on certain aspects of the game's narrative."

The Expanse: Osiris Reborn looks like it's carrying the best bits of Mass Effect forward, and in an encouraging move, the developers have been collaborating with David Gaider.

Of course, David Gaider is best known as the lead writer on Dragon Age: Origins, Dragon Age 2 and Dragon Age: Inquisition - he's also often credited as the architect of its dark fantasy world Thedas. Gaider's post-BioWare career saw him open his own game development house Summerfall Studios, which most recently released an ambitious roleplaying musical called Stray Gods.

But he's now lending a hand to a game that's not too dissimilar to BioWare's other hugely famous roleplaying series, while still working on his own games at Summerfall.

"Alongside my work at Summerfall, I've also been collaborating with the Owlcat Games team on The Expanse: Osiris Reborn, focusing on certain aspects of the game's narrative. The Expanse has long been one of my favourite series, and so obviously I jumped at the opportunity to be involved," he wrote on BlueSky.

"The Owlcat team has been so great, it's really such a treat. One thing I enjoy is how responsive they are to the fans," Gaider added, pointing to how the studio recently recast the male version of its protagonist in response to feedback. The game's reworked and re-designed Martian Captain is now voiced by Blythe Melin.

The Expanse: Osiris Reborn shouldn't be confused for the other very Mass Effect-y RPG coming out next year, Exodus. Though it's good to hear that both upcoming projects have some BioWare veterans on board, especially after the famed developer was shut down and had its own promising, actual Mass Effect game cancelled.

Bertie enjoyed what he played of the upcoming game in Eurogamer's The Expanse preview, but also had some concerns about the developer's use of generative AI.

In the brief clip, which can be viewed above, Replicants have taken over Los Angeles and are killing humans in broad daylight. Cora (Hunter Schafer) is humanity's last hope, as she volunteers to go undercover as a Blade Runner who is overseen by Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Replicant who is in the final weeks of her life.

"It's harder to look something in the eye than to kill it," Olwen says over a montage of dreary neo-futuristic violence. Another voice assures someone, most likely someone human, that what Cora's doing will "make the world ours again." Given how bleak things are, I'm not so sure. Especially considering that the final moments of the trailer see Olwen drive a pretty freaked-out Cora out into the desert, while telling her that she has to "see the lie" in front of her.

Created by Silka Luisa and executive-produced by Ridley Scott, the cast includes Dimitri Abold, Amy Lennox, Lewis Gribben, and Wil Coban. It's worth noting that, although Scott worked pretty closely with Luisa on the making of the series, Blade Runner 2099 is meant to be its own eight-episode standalone limited series... and that Ryan Gosling's K won't be popping up in a cameo or anything of that nature.

Blade Runner 2099 hits Prime Video on November 25. For more, check out our guide to the best shows on Prime Video.

#3796. Updated Xbox PC app promises 60% faster loading and easier access to games, but CEO Asha Sharma says there's "plenty more to do"

The Xbox PC app hasn't had the best track record in recent years, but Microsoft is promising that it's now much faster and easier to use than before.

Starting today, anyone part of the Xbox Insiders program can try out the new improvements. According to Microsoft, the updated Xbox PC app now boots up 60% faster, several pages can launch up to 50% faster, and in-app windows can open up to 65% faster. The company acknowledged that performance can vary based on your set up, internet connection, device, and so on.

The rest of the update involves "simpler navigation, updated filters, and new ways to organise your games," according to Xbox Wire, while social features are now included in the main navigation menu so you can start playing or chatting with friends quicker.

A faster Xbox PC app is certainly nice for players who regularly use it, though it's still missing a lot of the features that make Steam the go-to place to buy PC games. CEO Asha Sharma called the update "a meaningful improvement," but acknowledged there's still "plenty more to do."

Microsoft also said "it's easier to find what you're looking for" using the app's search function, and refreshed game cards and animations should give the platform "a cleaner look and feel."

Elsewhere, the revamped cloud gaming setup will roll out to even more people using web browsers, and more Xbox Insiders should hear about the program over the next few weeks. "The updated experience also makes it easier to find and play your games," the company said while bringing attention to its new light and dark modes. Supported smart TVs and VR headsets will get the updated cloud experience, as well.

Earlier this year, the console maker brought a selection of 'classic' games to PC for the first time ever - Blinx: The Time Sweeper, Conker: Live and Reloaded, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge and Fuzion Frenzy led the first batch. Mythic Achievements - the Platinum Trophy equivalent - went live for all Xbox players, too.

#3795. How to buy the store in Probably Stolen

Whether you are tired of dealing with the landlord and his oppressive price hikes or just want to unlock one of the many endings in Probably Stolen, saving enough to buy the store should be among your end-game goals.

But how much does the store cost? And most importantly, how can you unlock the ability to purchase it in the first place? Here’s how to buy the store in Probably Stolen.

You can buy the store in Probably Stolen by amassing any of the sums below before accepting the landlord’s offer at the end of the week. Don’t take the prices as a guarantee, though, as the store will progressively increase in value once you pass the 50-day mark, no matter your difficulty of choice.

If you don’t have the necessary Credits, a Loan Shark will keep his promise and visit your store a few days after you break past the 5.000 mark. He will come with a proposition, allowing you to purchase the store via a down payment and multiple weekly deposits. Upon making all payments, you will receive the documentation and close the deal.

Even if using the Loan Shark might be a good alternative for those looking to get the store early and unlock the Prodigious achievement in Probably Stolen, most of the player base considers it to be a bad deal in the long run, with investing in the right foundations and getting it done in a single payment being the safest option.

That rings even more true considering how, although inviting, all of the weekly payments part of the deal come with heavy interest and usually demand triple the amount of your rent at twice the risk.

Now that you truly own the store, don’t forget to also check out how to unlock all of the game’s remaining endings. We also recommend taking a look at our Eleanor quest guide so you can see her full story through and avoid any tragic mistakes.

Tomorrow, November 10, EVE Online is releasing a new expansion, Fractured Skies, and companion FPS EVE Vanguard is going into something Fenris Creations is calling a 24/7 alpha. Formal early access on Steam is coming late next year, but you can buy the game and play it through EVE's own client⁠—and it won't go away like prior playtests.

Tomorrow will also see Vanguard start to fulfill its promise as a linked game to EVE Online⁠—completing contracts in the multiplayer FPS will create military campaign opportunities players can find and act on in EVE—marking the return of a dream Fenris (formerly CCP Games) has pursued since the ill-fated PS3 shooter, Dust 514. I sat down with Vanguard game director Scott Davis and EVE design director Greg Hennessey to talk about what's coming tomorrow and further down the line.

From a pure gameplay perspective, Davis told me that NPC AI and new player onboarding are the biggest improvements in Vanguard since its last playtest. The NPC enemies inhabiting Vanguard's levels just weren't challenging enough, and while it's easy to make them better shots, the problem was more one of tactical depth.

"We had a lot of people bounce off the game pretty hard in July," Davis said of the other issue, Vanguard's new player experience. "I think we'd accidentally created the most hardcore extraction game of all time, because we had some awkward intricacies to how weapon upgrading and healing worked in the game." There will be more direct tutorializing to address this in tomorrow's Alpha, and a lot of thought has also gone into how Vanguard introduces its modes to players.

New players will be introduced through a full co-op/PvE mode, which will then unlock the PvEvP from the last playtest. The final mode sounds the most exciting and unique, though: Davis described it as a PvP-first "3v3v3 procedurally generated labyrinth, where you just go in and only one team can get out alive."

That sounds sick, and reminds me a bit of Marathon's Cryo Archive pinnacle activity. I'm encouraged by the variety of playstyle options Vanguard is offering: Marathon seems to have ultimately been sunk by its pure focus on hardcore PvP, while Vanguard might have an advantage attracting and holding a healthy playerbase with such varied modes.

The back of the box pitch for Vanguard is that what happens in the FPS will impact EVE Online's one-of-a-kind digital economy, and vice versa. I keep saying it's like the jocks (FPS guys) teaming up with the nerds (spreadsheet EVE guys), and people generally smile politely when I do.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

The 24/7 alpha is coming with a first version of that interoperability, with mission completion unlocking mining and combat activities in EVE Online. The next big step in this connection is planned for the second quarter of 2027. At that point, Fenris plans for Vanguard players to be able to declare allegiance with one of the four main empires in EVE, then have their mission progress contribute to the Military Campaign and Conquest systems introduced in EVE's latest two expansions.

Davis sees the empire allegiance system as a major step by Vanguard toward EVE's style of emergent player behavior. One thing he's looking forward to: Vanguard players adopting faction heraldry on their characters, and the sorts of Arc Raiders moments it may foment out in the wild. Maybe you hold fire on a stranger in PvEvP mode because you recognize you're both aligned with the same faction. Alternately, maybe you go out of your way to hunt down a player because they're aligned with an opposing empire.

I was curious if linking the two games had presented any technical difficulties, but both Davis and Hennessey told me it's been surprisingly smooth sailing. "We've sent up many flares ourselves before, but we haven't really had many messages back," Davis told me. "And I wouldn't call it a technical hurdle, because everyone's been working really hard and they know how to do it. But I think that there will be a champagne popping moment of getting those first messages back from EVE Online."

Hennessey, meanwhile, said it's less an issue of connecting the two games. Rather, he pointed out that making a game is hard, making two is twice as hard, and that these two games of very different genres have to align with and compliment each other.

But I hope it pays off, because this vision of two, nested live games changing and influencing each other in real time is like nothing else out there. If it speaks to you, you can wishlist EVE Vanguard on Steam or check out its paid alpha tomorrow through the EVE launcher.

#3793. GTA 6 party continues with Travis Scott, Cardi B, and more while you’ll be at home playing the game

Real world parties for an open world game.

It’s hard to believe, but Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally coming out next week, and Rockstar Games and PlayStation are throwing another big party in its honor.

Today, the companies announced GTA 6: The Festival, a special live concert at a convention center in Miami that’s “featuring a star-studded lineup of artists from the game and the official soundtrack,” including Travis Scott, Cardi B, Metro Boomin, and more, like French DJ duo Justice, who scored the game’s soundtrack.

Grand Theft Auto VI: The Festival, a special live event on November 21 at Mana Wynwood in Miami to celebrate the launch of GTAVI, featuring a star-studded lineup of artists from the game and the official soundtrack.More info: https://t.co/XRlfYFOk0H pic.twitter.com/fQyOU7I4gU

“This is a one-of-a-kind launch event that features two stages of nonstop music,” the website teases, confirming that entrants need to be 17 or older, and getting tickets means winning a literal lottery that will be drawn tomorrow at 6pm CT.

This sounds fun, and I’m sure it’ll be a great time, but I’m not really sure who the target demographic is for this sort of event. It’s definitely not GTA 6 players, right? Because when the event takes place next Saturday, Nov. 21, we’ll all be in Vice City playing through Jason and Lucia’s story as opposed to clubbing it up. Plus, can’t we just go to nightclubs in the game instead, and not have to deal with brain-pounding music, sweating profusely, and weird smells all around us?

I shouldn’t speak for all gamers, but I feel like I’m justified in saying that. GTA fans have been waiting over 13 years for this game, so while one night out feels like nothing in comparison, I think we’d all rather be playing the game itself, especially on its first weekend.

This is just another wildly outrageous form of advertising for GTA 6, which already has takeovers planned for the Miami Heat game on Nov. 18, the E11EVEN Miami nightclub turning into its Vice City counterpart, NINE1NINE Vice City, for a whole month, and a whole lot more.

You can read more about GTA 6: The Festival on Rockstar Games’ website, which is also filled with a slew of awesome screenshots of the actual game.

#3792. Xbox is testing a way to use your phone as a controller on smart TVs

Xbox is testing two new ways to play its cloud games, and one of them doesn't require a controller at all.

Announced on Xbox Wire on 4th November, the phone controller preview is rolling out on supported TVs wherever Xbox Cloud Gaming is available. The phone option - which works with both Android and iOS devices - lets you use your phone "as a controller when you don't have one nearby". Connect to your TV via QR code, and the controls open in your phone's browser.

The second preview, called cloud connect, is currently limited to the US and lets the new Xbox Nano controller talk to your cloud session over wi- fi instead of pairing directly with your TV to "help reduce input latency, so gameplay feels more responsive".

To try out the phone controls yourself, switch on Preview Features under Settings > Account in the latest version of the Xbox smart TV app.

Xbox has published a setup guide with full instructions, although you should note that both experiences "are still being tested", so the availability and supported games or devices "may be limited while [Xbox] learns from your feedback".

The company wants to "capture institutional knowledge" before it's too late

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nintendo of America is one of many companies investing in game preservation, and a new job listing gives us some insight into what those efforts look like. The company is looking to hire a "digital archivist" to build a library of historical material that can last for generations.

"We are seeking a Digital Archivist, Historical Systems to support the preservation, organization, and accessibility of historical hardware and software information," the company says in its job listing. "This role will design and implement a structured framework for organizing technical records, engineering documentation, source materials, and institutional knowledge related to legacy systems and platforms."

That's a lot of technical words for a position that ultimately boils down to 'build an internal library.' A company like Nintendo of America may have vast piles of historical development documents, advertising materials, and software prototypes on hand, but if nobody knows where any individual thing can be located, it may as well be lost altogether.

While many players might hear the phrase "game preservation" and think of efforts to ensure games are playable on modern devices, the field is far broader than that. Organizations like the Video Game History Foundation specialize in preserving not individual games, but development documents and other historical ephemera providing context on how historical games were developed, released, and played in their time.

Game publishers are starting to invest in this area themselves. PlayStation has a vast vault of historical materials, and Blizzard is building the same sort of archive. For the most part, these archives are never intended to be viewed by the public, but their work can help developers looking to build on historical games. Archived materials might, for example, show up as bonus features in remastered games.

Nintendo's digital archivist "will establish standards and processes that ensure historical information remains discoverable, usable, and preserved for future generations." The company describes this as a 12-month contract position, so it's presumably hoping that its hire will set up an archive and workflow that employees can then add to autonomously.

Perhaps the most notable duty in the job listing is this: "Interview subject matter experts and long-tenured employees to capture institutional knowledge." Nintendo's made a point of hanging onto longtime staff even as other companies lay off developers with decades of experience, but even in an environment that values experience many of gaming's most notable developers are reaching retirement age. Saving their stories and experience for the next generation is going to be a massive boon.

#3790. Wardogs Season 3 brings an urban map, Limited Mode, and a 185,000-account ban wave

Wardogs' Season 3 will launch on 12th November, complete with a new urban map, a new Limited Mode, and a ban wave targeting 185,000 accounts.

Developer Bulkhead confirmed the details earlier this week, revealing plans for a full wipe and progression changes that it hopes will "recapture the shared discovery and sense of achievement that defined" the 100-player tactical shooter when it first launched in Early Access.

The new map will focus on close-quarters fighting, and for a "more level playing field", players can dip into Limited Mode, which offers "an alternative way to experience" the game as it restricts weapons, ammunition, armour, and vehicles.

While the full list of restrictions is still being decided, it currently includes FMJ-only ammunition, a Tier 2 armour cap, and a reduced attack vehicle selection.

"The mode is designed to preserve the feel of early-to-mid-game combat and reduce the advantage offered by more powerful equipment," the team said.

Bulkhead also confirmed seasons are getting longer. From now on, they’ll last three months, giving players "more time to work towards their goals before each wipe and the development team more time to prepare future updates". Progression will also be "brought closer to the pace of Season 1", following the studio’s acknowledgement that Season 2 accelerated "the journey too aggressively".

"Season 3 is about giving players a new battlefield to learn together and a progression journey worth spending time on," said Bulkhead CEO Joe Brammer. "Longer seasons give everyone more room to reach their own goals, and give us the time to properly develop what comes next."

Alongside Season 3, Bulkhead revealed it has used machine learning to review is "activating further layers of its anti-cheat" after analysing 187 million hours of gameplay with help from machine learning. It says having close to four million unique players since launch gave it enough data to pull that work forward from next year.

"[E]xploiters, real-money traders, and gold-farming networks" have been permanently banned and lost their server-hosting privileges, and a player trust score is planned for 2027.

"Protecting the people who play Wardogs fairly is essential to everything we're building," Brammer added.

Bigger changes to the metagame, including a new progression system, are also due in 2027 as Bulkhead works towards Wardogs 1.0. Full Season 3 patch notes will be out before launch.

Wardogs launched in Steam Early Access on 10th September, and is due on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S in 2028.

Wardogs is one of the breakout successes of the year. In our early access Wardogs review, we said the game's mix of competitive shooters' best bits with something entirely of its own made it "a brilliantly refreshing take on the genre".

Not this time! Looks like Jeff has someone watching over him…🤫 pic.twitter.com/JEoAr7AmBt

EVE Online is about to have a big week, with the introduction of paid, 24/7 alpha access to companion FPS Vanguard, as well as a new expansion for the OG MMO, Fractured Skies. Both are launching tomorrow, November 10.

That expansion is bringing a bunch of new features⁠—updated HUD, new ships, and further tweaks to the new player experience added over the summer⁠—but when I spoke with EVE design director Greg Hennessey, he was most excited about coming changes to lowsec PvP, and what they'll offer both new and experienced players.

EVE is most famous for the big intrigues and betrayals of nullsec space, but Hennessey estimated that participants in the more structured, constant lowsec conflicts "are actually probably our strongest PVP players in general.

"Our nullsec players are the ones who want to plot for three years and go have a billion dollar war for a year. [Lowsec] players every day are like, let's go out and brawl. Let's just go lose some ships, boys. Let's get out there."

Hennessey characterized Fractured Skies as the "second in a trilogy of expansions" overhauling faction conflict in lowsec. The summer expansion, Cradle of War, added ongoing Military Campaigns players could pitch in with to affect an ongoing story. Fractured Skies will introduce a recurring climax to factional PvP, with the first such Conquest scheduled for February.

"You pick a faction, and for a season, you'll face off against another faction across that season," explained Hennessey. "You will fight to earn points, and all of that drives towards a scheduled final battle. We also know that when people think about EVE Online, they think about big battles in space, but they can be really hard to get into.

"When you start playing, you're like, how do I get into one? When do I show up? And that's kinda 3,000 hours in the end game. But every 10 weeks or so, you're gonna know: I can roll up with whatever I have and go shoot some structures and have a big fight."

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

So new players potentially get a smoother introduction to big fleet battles and ongoing participation in a conflict. As for old hands, Hennessey reckons that Conquests will introduce clear resolution and achievement to the constant churn of faction-based struggle.

"What we're saying is: You can win, and you will be recognized for this victory, and that will be recorded in history," he explained. "You'll be remembered for the [theoretical] five-year-long streak of Amar victories that happened. So we're giving them a sense of permanence, a sense of victory, and a sense of accomplishment that I think they felt has been lacking in their actual work or gameplay."

Hennessey also pointed out that Conquests won't exist in a vacuum: They'll impact resource and ship pricing in EVE's emergent economy, while outside forces will be able to influence Conquests in turn. Success in ongoing seasonal events will confer bonuses in the final blowout, but Hennessey pointed out that the underdog could always hire external help to make up the difference. And there's always the possibility someone intervenes and sows chaos just 'cos.

As for the final part of this trilogy of expansions, Hennessey was mum on details, but indicated that there would be a continued emphasis on getting new players to the cool parts of EVE without having to log 3,000 hours of playtime first. In the meantime, Fractured Skies will launch tomorrow through Steam, Epic, and EVE Online's own client.

#3787. Assassin's Creed is reportedly going to ancient Rome, while a mobile spin-off heads to Jerusalem

Ubisoft is reportedly working on two new Assassin's Creed games, and one of them is set in ancient Rome.

That's according to YouTuber Xj0nathan, who says the Rome game is codenamed Mars. He claims two sources with access to Ubisoft's backend systems backed up the information, and that the setting will likely be linked to the upcoming Assassin's Creed TV series.

The second game, codenamed Pocket, is said to be a mobile title set in Jerusalem. Xj0nathan claims it'll play a bit like Assassin’s Creed Valhalla’s Mastery Challenge, and look similar to the most recent Prince of Persia. The hero's mentor is apparently a character called Myriam.

Insider Gaming says it's heard the codenames too, but couldn't confirm them well enough to report them independently. It puts some of that down to the turbulence the franchise has gone through since former Assassin's Creed boss Marc-Alexis Côté left Ubisoft.

Last month, the outlet's sources also claimed Assassin's Creed Hexe, the next mainline game, had been delayed internally by another year, likely to 2028. Other reports claim we'll see it next year.

If Mars does move into full production, don't hold your breath - Insider Gaming doesn't expect us to hear anything about it until 2029 or 2030.

Assassin's Creed has visited Rome before, in 2010’s Brotherhood, but that was the Renaissance version of the city.

The leak comes less than a week after Ubisoft issued a statement about the future of the Assassin's Creed series, insisting there are currently no new remakes of the series' past games in the works.

Something you learn in 13 years of video game journalism is that some people react poorly to reading things they said. Being quoted can be scary. Now the words sound the way they did leaving your mouth, not the way they may have sounded inside your head.

Anyway, OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman recently complained that his remarks on a podcast, in which he bemoaned the inefficiencies of RAM sitting in personal PCs and not cooking away in AI data centers, were "taken out of context."

"From a global allocation perspective, actually it's quite terrible to have everyone have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer, and be used 5% of the time," he said. Later, Altman insisted, after quite some outcry, that "I actually do want the world to have tons of memory and people to put as much as they want in their computers."

Clearly, one software developer took this as a challenge. Enter: Ram-Altman, "A bash script that emails Sam Altman once a day to report the RAM he missed."

Developed (and shared on GitHub) by self-described network operations manager Iain Kay, Ram-Altman is a simple script that automatically informs Altman, at his email, that you have RAM and you are not using it.

"There is RAM in your computer. Right now. Just sitting there, in a personal computer, being personal. You may have thought of this as 'a computer working normally.' On a recent episode of Cheeky Pint, the CEO of OpenAI offered another view," the tool blurb reads.

"So we wrote a script. If your machine has more than 10% of its RAM available, it sends one email a day to let Sam know. It seemed only fair. He can't fix the problem if nobody tells him where the RAM is."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

A sample message that might be sent to Altman, signed "a concerned RAM owner," reads: "Please don't be alarmed, but there is 8.6 GiB of RAM on my desk that isn't in a data centre. That's 56.2% of what's installed here, and as far as I can tell it has no plans today."

If you're wondering, the tool only looks at 10% unused RAM or greater because, "below that, your machine has suffered enough." If you need me, I'll be closing 47 browser tabs.

#3784. Sony delays PlayStation's Pulse Elevate speakers indefinitely, less than a week before launch

Sony has delayed its Pulse Elevate wireless speakers indefinitely, less than a week before they were due to launch.

The news came in a 6th November update to Sony’s original announcement on the PlayStation Blog, first spotted by IGN. Quality testing has turned up a "production issue", Sony said, and there's no new release date yet.

"As part of our ongoing quality testing of Pulse Elevate speakers, we have identified a production issue with the product and have made the decision to delay the launch," the statement reads. "The additional time will allow us to ensure the product will deliver the experience we intended for our players. We apologise for the delay and appreciate your patience and understanding. We look forward to bringing Pulse Elevate to players soon."

The speakers were set to go on sale worldwide on 12th November, and pre-orders opened in September. It's unclear what, exactly, happens to those orders, but we'll update as and when we find out more.

Sony revealed Pulse Elevate in September 2025 as its first wireless speakers for desktop gaming. They sit alongside the Pulse Elite headset and Pulse Explore earbuds, and cost £199.99 ($219.99).

They connect to PS5, PC, Mac, and PlayStation Portal via PlayStation Link, and can pair with a phone over Bluetooth at the same time. There's also a microphone in the right speaker with what Sony calls "AI-enhanced noise rejection".

Midnight Black was due to be available everywhere, while the White version was limited to a handful of countries, including the UK.

Alongside the Pulse Elevate speakers, Sony revealed a range of hardware in September 2025, including a 27-inch gaming monitor that's coming only to the US and Japan.

Title Update 1.2.0 is coming to FC 27 on Nov. 10, and it includes major changes. EA Sports has already announced the highlights we can expect in this major patch, and there will be plenty of gameplay tweaks.

Let’s find out what to expect from the next major gameplay patch.

Gameplay is the main focus of this patch, and EA Sports has considered major community feedback.

Title Update v1.2.0 introduces our first gameplay adjustments for #FC27. Including changes to 95 Depth, fullback positioning, and more. Alongside key updates for Career Mode, FUT, and The Grounds.Read the full Pitch Notes here: https://t.co/QcjkIj9OgJ pic.twitter.com/DlkP0t4Asp

95 Depth will be nerfed, and the position of defenders will be adjusted. Unlike previous instances, they will now drop off sooner while still maintaining the higher line. This allows attackers to have more space to build their attacks.

Fullbacks used to drop deeper than intended when defending attacks. This has been adjusted, and fullbacks will now hold a firmer defensive line.

Similarly, attackers will do a better job at reading the opponent’s defensive line and make better runs to capitalize on the space.

The defensive line will hold a slightly higher position right after kick-off, making it easier to defend against opponents.

Auto-switching will be improved in loose ball scenarios, which also includes instances when a teammate performs a slide tackle, a headed pass, or when a shot misses the target.

Career Mode will also receive improvements in UI and other areas.

The patch will also feature plenty of minor fixes across multiple modes.

World of Warcraft: Forever made some changes to how dungeons work—rather than getting a bunch of XP from enemies in dungeons, you predominantly get experience points from the quests surrounding them.

Which is made slightly better for the fact that there are just more dungeons overall—so while you can't sit in dungeons until level 60, you can chain between those dungeons with minimal questing, though some questing is still basically mandatory if you care about being efficient.

This has been a point of consternation. Any brief visit over to the r/classicwow subreddit leads to a raft of complaint threads about dungeon XP, though other communities do vary. It should be mentioned that a singular subreddit isn't reflective of the game's entire population, mind—but it is notable how upset the dungeon-loving slice of WoW's playerbase is.

To try and soothe that ache, Blizzard's gone ahead and buffed the XP gain: "At about 11:05 PST today, we deployed a hotfix that increased kill experience in dungeons by 50%, so it feels better to go back in for more runs," writes community manager Kaivax. "Happy dungeon crawling, and good luck with those Deviate Hides!"

That 50% number isn't actually too much, mind—it's a 50% increase to the current value. So let's say you were getting 40 XP from a mob: You're now getting 60.

For the record, I'm a touch on the fence about this one. I do think that the amount of XP from enemies alone was kind of unhealthy for the game. You do want those repeat runs to give a decent batch of experience, not just for folks who would rather spend their time rinsing dungeons with their mates, but also so healers and tanks have a reason to come back to them and to keep the dungeon-delver's population healthy after the launch week rush.

On the other hand, I'm kind of fine with dungeons giving a huge batch of XP up front and then not being the best way to level thereafter. It's ultimately okay if World of Warcraft: Forever is a videogame about questing or exploring the open world.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

But I can see the other side of the coin: The major problem is that Forever's also been pitched as a game about returning to the Azeroth you knew, but with a shinier coat of paint. And for some WoW players, that Azeroth predominantly took place in instanced content with a bunch of their buddies over Teamspeak or Ventrilo. I don't think they're wrong for feeling hard done-by.

If you were to put the balancing in my hands (you shouldn't) I'd say dungeon grinding ought to be just a little behind questing as an XP source, given you get such a massive bump of XP from dungeon quests on your first run. Still worthwhile, but nothing that's going to outpace playing to Forever's strengths.

I just hope this design isn't completely walked back, though, because I think Forever will be a stronger game if it sticks to its guns, even if that's not to everyone's tastes—because games are generally more interesting when they do that.

#3781. Star Wars Zero Company studio Bit Reactor lays off staff, a month after bringing furloughed developers back

"While it stings, I'm really proud of what we built together."

Star Wars Zero Company developer Bit Reactor has laid off an unspecified number of staff, a month after bringing some of its furloughed team back to work.

Several developers announced on LinkedIn on Friday, 6th November, that they had been let go, as first reported by Bespin Bulletin. Bit Reactor hasn't said how many people are affected.

Among them is senior environment artist Ryan Lopez, who spent three and a half years working on Zero Company, from pre-production to launch, and was laid off after a three-month furlough. UI engineer Tyler Eichten, who worked on much of the on-screen UI for the game's tactical missions, and Ryan Mosher from the QA team have also confirmed they were let go.

"While it stings, I'm really proud of what we built together," Lopez wrote. "It was a privilege to ship a game with you."

Bit Reactor furloughed most of its staff in the weeks before Zero Company launched on 27th August, with one source putting the figure at roughly 80 percent. The studio appeared to have run out of money just short of release.

The game did well regardless, and is thought to have sold more than a million copies within a month. Then, in a message shared on Bluesky on 7th October, CEO Greg Foertsch said the studio had "started the process of returning more of our team back to work". Asking staff to step away so close to launch was "an incredibly difficult decision", he said, "but one that was necessary to help us eventually bring as many people back as possible".

It's thought more than half the studio returned, though not everyone went back on full pay. It's not clear whether any of those who returned were among the people laid off this week.

In Eurogamer's Star Wars Zero Company review, we awarded the game four out of five stars, saying, "an already winning genre is matched with the perfect setting in this earnest, heartfelt, smart and slightly ramshackle turn-based tactics gem".
