#3780. Hideo Kojima’s PHYSINT is somehow looking like a weirder Metal Gear Solid, and I’m all for it

Hideo Kojima and his PHYSINT project made headlines earlier this year when both moved from PlayStation to Xbox, but it’s still years off from releasing.

Kojima’s team is currently working horror title OD: Knock, but PHYSINT is on deck as an action-espionage title starring Bill Skarsgård as the main protagonist, plus Charlee Fraser, Dong Lee, and Godzilla Minus Zero’s Minami Hamabe. All accounts say it may be a spiritual successor to Kojima’s Metal Gear franchise, and new information only solidifies that.

PHYSINT at the Kojima Productions Beyond The Strand Exhibition! 👀 pic.twitter.com/UdRjXyKgbU

A special exhibit running for about a month in Tokyo to celebrate Kojima Productions’ 10th anniversary gave us a new look at concepts for PHYSINT, and yeah, welcome back, Metal Gear.

Along with an amazing sculpture of different appearances of Bill Skarsgård’s character, there are also two very distinct-looking mech designs, as shown in photos in the Twitter/X post above taken at the exhibit.

One looks like a Metal Gear, and there’s no other way to describe it: a bipedal tank with a sphere shape on one “arm” and what looks like a gun on the other. It looks like several other Metal Gear prototypes from MGS history, and something that easily could’ve appeared in the Konami franchise.

And then there’s the other one, which looks like a mech that comes equipped with three longer legs, akin to something like the alien ships seen in War of the Worlds with Tom Cruise. And at the bottom, a human man, showing the massive scale of the mech, towering well over the figure below it.

I’m all in, man. It just sucks that we’re so far off from seeing this title, but any sort of remnants of Metal Gear weirdness stuck in Kojima’s head with an actor like Skarsgård at the forefront? Sounds like gold to me, but we’re still several years from seeing it release, so hopefully OD can tide us over til then.

It's just me in the office today. Normally that's fine. I don't mind the quiet, and I can be as messy as I like without Jacob tutting at me. Today is different. Today that comes with a healthy dose of fear. Fear because I have to lift the MSI Maestro 900R case up onto the test bench desk, and I don't think Paul, the oddball security guard way downstairs at the front desk, will hear me if I scream because my spine has snapped. It's a two person job and I'm very much a one-person team in PC Gamer towers today. I have managed to get it situated on the desk, but I can certainly feel it in my near fifty-year-old back muscles. *Spasm*. And when you need another human on hand every time you want to shift your gaming PC about, I think that says a lot about both this MSI case and who it's aimed at.

In short, I think you need to be someone who has their own staff.

That's partly a dig at its sheer scale—this thing is chomk with a capital CHOMK—but also at the fact only the very wealthy are going to consider this chassis a worthwhile casing for their gaming PC. This is a $700 (£800) PC case and that feels, on one hand, par for the course in these days of hyper-expensive everything, but also faintly anachronistic.

As always with the case reviewing process, I built a new PC inside it, and it only felt right to be doing so with high-end gear. So, I picked from the review kit that was in the cupboard: a MSI Godlike X with a Ryzen 9 9950X3D seemed appropriate, along with some 64 GB of G.Skill ULL memory and an RTX 5090. And that's when this whole endeavour started to feel like something from a bygone age.

Before, when I'd do a high-end build, it felt exciting in a way that was both special—because I could never spend out on such premium parts myself—but also still kind of achievable, too, because the money wasn't so far beyond the realms of decency that you couldn't imagine someone normal pushing their budget a little far to get this sort of kit. But looking at the parts going into this, it's around $12,000 worth of kit at least. And that feels well beyond a normal PC gamer and into faintly distasteful territory.

But, in all honesty, I'm not even totally convinced the MSI Maestro 900R really deserves its place in such company. Sure, it's elegant in black and gold trim, but there are odd touches here and there which belie the super premium pricing. The most egregious is something I picked out when I saw a preview case out at Computex this year, and that's the top flair on the case. The metal 'lid' only covers half of the dust filter for the 360 mm cooler I'd mounted to the top, and that filter is just a flimsy plastic one I wouldn't really want on display.

I also question the utility of having the motherboard and GPU's outputs all out of reach in the centre of the case, behind tempered glass shields. There are a ton of Type-A and Type-C USB ports on the front panel, but still it's a lot of effort to get to the I/O panel of your motherboard. And don't get me started on the PSU buried right in the back of the case, with impossible-to-reach switches and plug sockets.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

But there are things I like, too. The wraparound glass does look great, and I loved having so much space to work in when building into the rig. And to have that full central motherboard tray be completely removable was a treat, as well. You essentially have your own little test rig there, so you can make sure everything works before you do the full install. It's neat. As is the final build.

But honestly, this feels more like a chassis you might buy for someone else to build into. Because you're Mr. or Mrs. Moneybags and don't want to get your hands dirty doing manual labour and just want to have a high-end rig to play your games on in something that stands like a glass and gold monolith in the bespoke gaming room of your palace.

✅ You only have a passing knowledge of what's in your bank account: If you watch the pennies this isn't a chassis for you, but if you don't—and you're into the black, glass, and gold aesthetic, and have the space—then maybe it's worth considering.

❌ You need regular access to your mobo's I/O panel: The Maestro 900R hides it all away inside the case, meaning you have to open it up to get at the back of your motherboard.

You will get a super-clean final build out of the Maestro 900R, and it will look stunning for the most part. But when you get up close there are some parts which don't feel totally premium, and the price is as much of a barrier as the tempered glass side panels are to actually getting to your system's I/O ports.

Regular: E-ATX / ATX / Micro-ATX / Mini-ITX

1 x LED Switch Button · 1 x Mic-in / Audio-out · 1 x Power Button · 4 x USB 5Gbps (Type-A) · 4 x USB 10Gbps (Type-C) · 1 x USB 20Gbps (Type-C)

Top: 4 x 120 mm / 3 x 140 mm / 3 x 160 mm · Side: 6 x 120 mm · Bottom: 4 x 120 mm / 3 x 140 mm / 3 x 160 mm

Top: 120 / 140 / 240 / 280 / 360 / 420 mm · Side: 120 / 240 / 360 mm · Bottom: 120 / 140 / 240 / 280 / 360 / 420 mm

695 x 379 x 671 mm / 27.36 x 14.92 x 26.42 inches

Net weight: 33 kg / 72.75 lbs · Gross weight: 38 kg / 83.78 lbs

The key things to note are the sheer size of this beast. At well over 30 kilos, this is a massive chassis and when you've built a rig into it, that weight only goes up. It's a two-person job shifting this thing around, as my poor back can attest to.

The other thing is that it is really pleasing to build into. Thanks, in part, to the size of the case and the space you have to work in, but also because of that central motherboard tray. It is effectively a standalone test bench, and makes putting the board itself in place a doddle. It's also rotatable, so you can orient your system inside however you'd like. And because all the external cables need to be routed around from inside to outside anyways, you don't have to worry about where the mobo's I/O is going to go because it'll largely be inaccessible anyways.

To help this you have four 10 Gbps Type-C USB ports on the front of the case, along with a further 20 Gbps Type-C with 60 W power delivery, and four 5 Gbps USB Type-A ports. That does salve some of the pain of not being able to access your motherboard's back panel.

The other useful thing is that it comes with three 160 mm reverse blade fans, so the intakes on the base don't show their ugly side and ruin the high-end aesthetic.

Installation is an absolute joy… until it isn't. That occurs towards the end of the build, but at the start it really is all fun and games. The removable fan tray makes it easy to get your 360 mm radiator in place and the scale of the case means there's always space to work in when you've pulled the tool-free side panels off.

That motherboard tray is excellent, too. I was a big fan of that when I saw it out at Computex, and have been just as impressed now I've used it properly. The issue is that if you want to test out the components you've bought for this build using it as a standalone test bench, you will have to largely break it all down again before you can jam it into the system itself. But that's to be expected, and being able to just get your motherboard, CPU, cooling bracket, SSD, and RAM in place free from even the modest constraints of this massive rig is a real boon.

The installation pain is rear-loaded, however, and once you've got everything inside and wired up internally it then becomes a game of figuring out how the hell you're actually going to attach this thing up to either power or a monitor. There is no real back to this case, with the wraparound tempered glass surrounding the entire plane you mount the motherboard too. That means all the cables, from power, to display, to networking and anything else going into the back of your board, need to be routed out of some grommeted holes on the underside of the case.

It means you'll likely need a longer HDMI or DP cable than you have right now, because it needs to be routed in and around the inside of the case to get to the vertically mounted graphics card, which cuts a lot off its length. And you're unlikely to be sitting this on a desktop given its girth, so it's going to need to stretch from the ground up. Similarly, the power cable for the PSU has to be squeezed into the case, and if you're using a large PSU—such as the MSI MEG Ai1600T brick I've been using—then that doesn't give you a lot of space to attach its fat plug.

But that lack of a busy, cable-heavy backside to the case does really aid the aesthetic. The shroud (which is sadly quite flimsy plastic) that covers the rear of the vertically mounted GPU and the rear of the motherboard hides all the cables that sprout from their outputs as they're fed out the underside of the case, and that gives it a really clean finish. Inside, it looks like there is almost nothing connecting the components, leaving them looking like they're floating around inside. The MSI Godlike X motherboard only helped this by hiding a lot of its power cabling, too.

The angled reverse-bladed fans on the bottom intake are slightly angled, which allows you to see them in all their RGB LED glory, but that, coupled with the angling of the top radiator mount, makes it feel even bigger inside. I really like the full wraparound tempered glass, too. It really gives it a showpiece aesthetic, which I can see being used at a bunch of PC trade show booths in the future.

What slightly ruins that aesthetic, however, is the exposed plastic dust cover on the top of the case. The metal cover, which slots on without screws, only partially covers the things, leaving it open to be eyeballed. And it's not a great look. Likewise, the plastic shroud covering the cables inside looks and feels flimsy. It's the same with the power and LED buttons on the front panel. They look like they could have come from any $50 chassis, as does the lightbar on the rear side of the case's top.

It is not the most expensive PC chassis you can buy on Newegg right now. But that's mostly because Newegg's marketplace is an odd place to be and there are a ton of Hatsune Miku Asus cases on there with four-figure price tags, and I can't figure out why. There's also a $1,000 Asus ProArt chassis on there, but you can also just buy that for $300 direct from Newegg if you'd rather. Which is a roundabout way of me saying that it is pretty much the most expensive chassis you can buy on Newegg without delving into the murky realms of the marketplace.

And, personally, I find it hard to reconcile any notions of value against the MSI Maestro 900R beyond the sheer mass of the thing. Were we going by size and weight, then, I guess it's a match for the Asus ProArt PA602. That's half the weight and half the price, so on a purely per-gram metric, it's all evens Antoine Griezmanns.

But in real terms, it's a massive, expensive case, that I struggle to find genuine ways to justify its cost. There are some neat features, such as that mobo tray, but also some genuine points of frustration that would have me not actually wanting to clothe my PC parts in its black, gold, and glass surrounds. I'm happy with my—what seems to be rather diminutive now—Hyte Y70 Touch. Again, it's half the price, but at least I can get at my PC bits and not break my spine picking it up off the ground.

4. Best budget compact: Thermaltake S100 TG Snow Edition

You will get a super-clean final build out of the Maestro 900R, and it will look stunning for the most part. But when you get up close, there are some parts which don't feel totally premium, and the price is as much of a barrier as the tempered glass side panels are to actually getting to your system's I/O ports.

#3776. Best WoW Forever classes

There's 9 Classes to choose from in WoW: Forever, and a lot of factors to consider.

The nine Classes of World of Warcraft: Forever are the same ones vanilla launched with in 2004, and they look nothing like what we have in Retail more than 20 years later. But Forever reimagines the vanilla experience, and Blizzard wants to “upgrade” how the Classes feel this time around.

The goal is for Classes to feel as balanced as possible without ruining how interesting their playstyles are, so Forever had a starting roster that felt rather nostalgic but still new enough to be unpredictable. But since Classes are made to feel and play differently from each other, you’d eventually be drawn to certain Classes for specific playstyles.

All Classes in Forever have something to offer, and they’re all versatile enough to offer more than two playstyles (through Specializations) even if they seem to be locked to a specific role. Staples you’re likely familiar with include:

Some Classes also provide some variety due to their mechanics:

Gold is not an easy currency to acquire in your Forever experience, especially as you level up (sometimes even with an alt!). Before you get your first Gold piece, you need to get through your Coppers and Silvers first. And with some of the game’s best gear, consumables, and materials locked behind a lot of Gold, you’d want to get as much Gold as fast as possible.

In principle, here’s how you often farm Gold in Forever, and this extends to the core World of Warcraft experience:

Among the Classes, here are standouts when it comes to Gold farming:

Of the rulesets in Forever, you might find yourself gravitating towards the Normal or PvE experience first. This is where most standard-fare open-world adventuring, and where raids and dungeons attract the most number of players. Besides Level 60, getting geared up for these PvE experiences is part of your capstones as you reach the higher levels.

There’s always room for pretty much any Class in a PvE party, but you might find some Classes preferred over others due to their inherent capabilities. Here’s a quick breakdown of where Classes usually fit in a PvE group:

You’d sometimes want a Class that is the best at something, but there are Classes with specs versatile enough to let them adjust combat strategies on the fly. These are hybrid roles, and some Classes excel at them:

Compared to hybrid roles, damage in PvE is allocated to Classes whose sole focus is to dish out as much DPS as possible. They are often glass cannons in that respect, so it’s the job of hybrid roles to make sure they remain alive long enough to actually kill mobs and demolish bosses.

Mages and Warlocks remain the strongest in the DPS caster categories, and your party can’t go wrong with either:

The same goes for Rogues and Hunters, but for melee DPS:

There’s no use working hard to fight in a dungeon when you’re dead as soon as the boss dishes out its AOE. And this is also the reason why the pressure’s on for healers to do their work properly, as it’s painfully obvious when the healers aren’t pulling the numbers they need since everyone else runs away to heal on their own. That, or a party wipe.

Thankfully, if you’re looking to train as a healer, you only really have four Classes you can focus on:

If you want to sink your teeth into PvP in Forever, you might notice that you’re getting into not one playstyle but actually three different types of mechanics. When you turn on your World PvP, anyone from another faction can fight you wherever, so if you can’t handle surprises, then you’re a goner.

Alternatively, there are PvP matches you can prepare for. Battlegrounds are faction-based matchups on instanced maps with point-based mechanics. Then there are duels, which are pretty much arranged fights between you and someone else.

The suggestions below will be based on what we can theorycraft with the Talent Trees, and what can be observed with Level 1 to 30 fights. Until we get to the real endgame in a couple of weeks, we can’t be 100% sure.

World PvP happens in the open, so the most ideal PvP Classes to take on enemies in the wild are the ones equipped for surprises.

Marksmanship/Survival Hunters specialize in long-range ambushes, which means they can run if they feel like they’re overwhelmed. With Track Humanoids on the map, they can set up slows and traps so targets never reliably reach them. And with Dismember, Sonic Blast, and Viper Sting in the mix, Hunters can pick targets easily… assuming they strike first. If Hunters are jumped on, they hardly have any way to disengage.

Druids and Rogues use the same formula here, in that they strike from the shadows and overwhelm enemies to submission:

The Frost Mage is interesting, as they’re only as devastating as the movement debuffs they can dish out. In theory, a Mage controls PvP with freezes and slows, then finishes with Ice Lance and Frostbolt. But if a target knows their mobility, the Mage can find it difficult to keep up.

Suppose you want the kind of PvP where someone invites you to a fight, and you duke it out fair and square, tournament-style. That means the Classes to choose are ideally built to target just one threat and defend against attacks that target only you. In that case, great Class picks would be:

Depending on the map, Battlegrounds are either capture the flag (Warsong Gulch), resource races (Arathi Basin, Darkspear Islands), or large-scale battles (Alterac Valley). Their objectives might differ, but the setup is the same – you’re all part of a team. This means the best Classes are both team players and built to kill:

#3775. Missing teenager rescued after reaching out to another player in Among Us

"Our priority in this case was the safe return of the minor victim."

A teenager who went missing in Utah more than 17 months ago has been rescued from a home in Oregon after she got in touch with another young player in Among Us.

According to a federal criminal complaint reported by Newsweek and KUTV (via IGN), the girl, who was 15 when she disappeared from Garden City, Utah, on 29th May 2025, began chatting with another teenager in Among Us on or around 15th October this year.

The pair later moved their conversation to a different social media app, where she told them who she was and that she was being held against her will in Oregon. She had been given a phone with no cellular data, which meant she could only get online via wi-fi.

The other teen told their parent, who contacted the FBI on 1st November. Agents listened in on a video call between the parent and the girl, and she was recovered from the house later that day. She is now 17.

Adam Hunter Harmel, 39, of Huntington, Oregon, was arrested during a traffic stop.

According to the US Attorney's Office for the District of Utah, he allegedly met the girl online in May 2025, then drove to Utah to pick her up and took her back to his home across state lines. He was charged on 2nd November with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity, and made his first court appearance in Boise, Idaho, on 4th November.

"Our priority in this case was the safe return of the minor victim," said US Attorney Melissa Holyoak. "Those who allegedly exploit and prey upon the most vulnerable members of our communities will be relentlessly investigated and held accountable."

Utah's US Attorney's Office stresses that a complaint is merely an allegation, and that all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

Researching and writing this story gave me massive deja vu, because what Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick said today about AI's evolving role in game development sounds like a re-wording of what every other C-suite executive has said about AI in game dev. In case you have somewhere to be, the TLDR is that Zelnick says AI will make game development easier but won't replace human creativity.

I don't want to minimize the importance of Zelnick, the guy at the top of the company funding the biggest entertainment launch of all time with GTA 6, talking about what could be the most consequential technological advancement since the internet, but decades of on-the-job media training have certainly worked their magic in this case.

In Take-Two's latest earnings call, Zelnick is asked about AI's influence on game development, and he begins his answer with this earth-shattering admission: "Look, technology benefits us."

Facing down a group of investors he's forced to answer to as the head of a publicly traded company, it's understandable that Zelnick wants to play it safe when discussing emergent technology, so I guess I should practice gratitude that he gave as lengthy an answer as he did here. Still, pound for pound this might be the highest ratio of words to meaning I've ever seen.

"We've always created our entertainment inside computers, with technology. All advances have benefited us, and I don't expect that that will change. In fact, I hope it'll accelerate. I think at the same time, what we're known for here is the desire to make the best entertainment on earth, and more often than not we succeed," Zelnick says, attributing the creativity of Take-Two studios to "human creativity" and "harnessing technology," which he expects to continue "in the future."

"Undoubtedly, some of the most recent technological advances that you've seen have made it easier to create assets. That is consistent with the story of our business. When I started in interactive entertainment, longer ago than I would like to say, it was really difficult to create an asset in a computer. Today, it's a whole lot easier."

Even here, he doesn't say AI specifically made asset creation easier, just "recent technological advances." Regardless, he draws a line at technology as a replacement for good old fashioned human creativity. "But you know what's not easier? Making a big hit. Making a big hit was hard then, it's hard now, and it's going to be hard in the future. And hit creation remains the purview of human beings."

If you have a high-end RTX 50-series graphics card then kudos to you. You either got in there early and avoided the massive price hikes that followed, or you managed to get a second mortgage and pick one up anyways. But either way, you're going to want to protect your investment because replacements are hard and expensive to find. And it looks like you really need to protect that investment because there are still regular cases of melting 12+4 pin power cables.

This latest (via Uniko's Hardware) serves as a reminder that getting a cable monitoring solution is a good way to protect your expensive graphics card, as user Edistonian2 notes in a recent reddit thread on the ThermalGrizzly sub. They note that they picked up an RTX 5090 in June and subsequently grabbed a WireView Pro II monitor to keep it safe.

The WireView noted odd current behaviour with two of the pins, while HWInfo said it was fine and a Gemini chat suggested it was an issue with the monitor. I'm sure that's what Nvidia would say, too... So they replace their WireView with a new one, and still get the current issues on pin four. So they removed the cable entirely and the image up top is what was happening on the PSU end of the wire.

They've since picked up another cable and swapped to the other GPU power port on the GPU and so far everything is fine, but it just shows that there are still power issues going on with these cables and a monitoring system can be a worthwhile step in between finding your power leads or plugs melting, or your GPU going up in a puff of smoke.

Now, it's not the cheapest method—the WireView Pro II is $190 at Amazon right now—but that is chump change in relation to the ~$8,000 you might have to spend on a replacement RTX 5090. There are also cheaper alternatives, such as Cooler Master's GPU Shield, which is $50, and the Super Flower 12+4 pin OCP Dongle.

Whichever you choose, as the pricing crisis continues for high-end cards, that's going to be a small price to pay to save something catastrophic happening to your expensive silicon.

#3772. Saving Mass Effect would take $200m+, says BioWare co-founder

Anyone hoping to buy Mass Effect from EA and finish what BioWare started needs to get saving now, as it could cost over $200 million (£150m).

That's according to BioWare co-founder Trent Oster, who reckons that's what a new Mass Effect game would need to meet fans' expectations.

"The scary component of Mass Effect is the audience is going to want the best of 'AAA' development," Oster said on Twitter/X, as spotted by GamesRadar.

The scary component of Mass Effect is the audience is going to want the best of “AAA” development. Rough ballpark (based on contemporaries) is $200M+. That is a big number to commit up front. There has to be a bigger plan in place for the IP to make the math work.

"Rough ballpark (based on contemporaries) is $200M+. That is a big number to commit up front. There has to be a bigger plan in place for the IP to make the math work."

He did add that it could be done for less, though. "That said, I think it can be done well for less than that amount with a disciplined approach and an experienced team," Oster said.

"I think a game could be done cheaper, if you kept it simple and hit the big beats," he added in a separate tweet. "It wouldn’t be what the team described in the Universe concept. The big push would be getting the IP free. The fans deserve more than one game."

I think a game could be done cheaper, if you kept it simple and hit the big beats. It wouldn’t be what the team described in the Universe concept. The big push would be getting the IP free. The fans deserve more than one game.

Oster's comments come as the #SaveMassEffect campaign continues to grow following EA's decision to close BioWare and cancel Mass Effect 5. Fans want EA to keep making Mass Effect games, or hand the series over to a studio that will.

Oster has backed the campaign too. "I love seeing all the energy around #SaveMassEffect," he wrote on 4th November. "I think there is a still a great thesis for a well-funded RPG developer who can deliver. Makes me want to get some of the original band back together."

EA has not confirmed whether or not it would consider selling the IP.

The petition created to save BioWare's well-loved sci-fi RPG, Mass Effect, topped 185,000 signatures in just days. It's now exceeded 317,000. Joe Smith, credited with starting the petition, isn't necessarily asking EA to change its mind about BioWare; instead, the petition calls for "decisive action by committing to the continued development of Mass Effect".

We said a sad farewell to BioWare last month. The closure, which came just months after Saudi Arabia's $55bn leveraged buyout of EA, was anticipated by experts, but drew widespread condemnation and messages of sympathy from across the industry.

A new report claims EA closed BioWare because it was forced to choose between investing in one of two sci-fi projects: a new Mass Effect game or a new Star Wars Battlefront game. And it chose the latter.

Fans are trying other routes to keep BioWare's doors open, too. Canadian fans of the studio have escalated their grievances to the governmental level, calling on the Canadian Government to step in and save the studio from closure, seemingly after Canada's New Democratic Party leader Avi Lewis called on the government to do so.

#3770. DC Comics movies may undergo yet another reset with James Gunn and Peter Safran replaced by former MCU producer

James Gunn and Peter Safran are out as the co-CEO’s of DC Studios, the main team behind projects like Superman, Clayface, Lanterns, and Peacemaker.

The duo are being replaced by Jeremy Latcham, who made his name at Marvel Studios from the very beginning, working under Kevin Feige. And so, it appears that DC’s new overlords at Skydance after its merger with Paramount are looking for some more money out of this whole situation.

“James and Peter began a new era for DC Studios, guiding it through a major transformation and bringing audiences fresh chapters of beloved stories, including Superman, Lanterns and Creature Commandos,” Skydance CEO David Ellison said. “We’re grateful for the passion and care they brought to this work, and for the lasting mark they’ve left on DC.”

Gunn and Safran’s approach to creating self-contained stories rather than an interconnected MCU-like universe had varying returns, but the duo will end their tenure on Dec. 1 before continuing on in their roles for Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow. Anything beyond that is still a question.

“We’re thrilled to welcome Jeremy to DC Studios,” Ellison continued. “As part of the founding team behind the Marvel Cinematic Universe, he helped define the modern superhero movie and powered some of the biggest, most beloved comic book adaptations of our time. We can’t wait to see the stories he’ll bring to life, and how he’ll help build the future of DC for fans everywhere.”

Latcham’s resume is strong, joining Marvel Studios all the way back in 2004 and working in production on such films as Iron Man, Iron Man 2, The Avengers, Guardians of the Galaxy, Avengers: Age of Ultron, andSpider-Man: Homecoming. He will “will lead DC’s film, television and animation slate, overseeing the creative pipeline, along with production, talent and strategy,” according to The Hollywood Reporter.

“DC’s pantheon of characters is among the most iconic in American popular culture,” said Latcham in a statement. “I’ve had the privilege to help bring some of the most celebrated superhero stories to life on the big screen, and I’m excited and honored for the opportunity to now lead DC Studios into its next era. The chance to steward the incredible cast of DC characters to the screen in a way that excites lifelong fans while introducing their timeless stories to the next generation is a massive responsibility that I do not take lightly.”

And so DC fans are left wondering what’s next, again, after seemingly yet another reset following Gunn taking over from Zack Snyder’s “SnyderVerse” set of films that were extremely hit or miss (mostly miss).

Will Latcham continue on the path that Gunn and Safran began, or will we get yet another do-over? Don’t forget, DC Studios still has The Batman: Part II releasing next year (in theory), and who knows if that’s its own thing or connected or otherwise. Five years between Batman movies should not happen, but, alas.

“Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision, Gunn and Safran said in a joint statement. “In that time, we helped restore Superman to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with Peacemaker, Creature Commandos, Lanterns and Clayface. “We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with.” Gunn had a whole lot more to say on Threads.

I think Gunn and Safran deserved more time to build something special, because Superman was great, Clayface was well-received and turned a profit on a small budget, and fans seem to love Lanterns as well. I always felt like there doesn’t need to be a massive, MCU-like interconnected universe with post-credits scenes in DC, but it appears that Skydance feels differently.

#3769. Phasmophobia players raise over $230,000 for heart charity, more than double last year's total

The Phasmophobia community has raised more than $230,000 (around £173,000) for the American Heart Association, more than doubling last year's total.

Developer Kinetic Games announced the final figure for this year's Ghost Hunts for Hearts event on 6th November. The charity drive ran from 26th October to 2nd November, and more than 500 streamers signed up to take part. That's the biggest turnout yet for a creator fundraiser run by Heart Liive, the American Heart Association's streaming initiative.

Last year's event raised a little over $100,000.

Congratulations, Ghost Hunters, you've surpassed the community target and raised over $200,000 for our friends at @Heart_Liive!Your kindness and generosity will not go unrewarded, log in to Phasmophobia before the 15th November to claim the Animated AHA Advocate ID Card &… pic.twitter.com/KFQKaqXNCl

Streamers who fundraised could hand out an event-exclusive Advocate ID Card and Badge to their viewers as a Twitch Drop. Kinetic set a target of $200,000 at the start of the week, and once players sailed past it, an animated version of the card and badge set unlocked for all.

"The Phasmophobia community never fails to amaze us, and this year they've outdone themselves," said Tom Dent, lead social media and player experience manager at Kinetic Games. "Thank you to every streamer, viewer and player who took part."

Phasmophobia launched in Early Access in September 2020, and sends teams of up to four players into haunted locations to gather evidence of what's lurking there.

The studio also launched a publishing arm, Kinetic Publishing, earlier this year. Its first game, the starship job simulator Contact Protocol, is due out in spring 2027.

Phasmophobia is available in Early Access on Steam, PS5, PS VR2, and Xbox Series X/S. It's also coming to Nintendo Switch 2, although we still don't quite know when.

Earlier this year, Kinetic Games confirmed Phasmophobia's 1.0 launch had slipped from this year into 2027, as the studio said it was prioritising quality over speed following a rocky reception to its Player Character Update. The studio ended up apologising to players for issues with the long-awaited update, admitting it "missed the mark" and "didn't deliver on our promises to you".

In partnership with West Coast Customs (remember Pimp My Ride?) for the anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto 6, Rockstar Games has brought the legendary Grotti Cheetah sports car into the real world. And you’ll only need about £1 million to pick it up. That’s about $1,344,250 in US dollars, by the way.

Here’s your chance to own a part of automotive & gaming history! We’re incredibly proud to have partnered with Rockstar Games® to bring the custom in-game Grotti Cheetah from ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ to life. See the full details: https://t.co/kakQSnoh96 pic.twitter.com/2CkYUtjEqF

“Few cars epitomize GTA quite like the Grotti Cheetah,” said the car’s listing on the website for Selfridges, a UK-based retail chain that’s selling the one of a kind vehicle. “For the launch of GTA 6, Rockstar Games collaborated with West Coast Customs to bring an icon to The Corner Shop. Painted in Vice City’s signature pink and blue hues, this customized retro sports car is available to purchase for £1 million via Selfridges Personal Shopping.”

The listing then links to a contact page where only those with bank accounts way, way, WAY bigger than mine will be taken seriously when it comes to owning the one-of-one recreation.

I can’t even fathom what happens when it comes to buying something like this. Do they just take the first offer, or do they go for the best offer available? Why is it not going to auction? #3767. Ocarina of Time remake datamine suggests Master Quest is on the way

Ocarina of Time's notoriously tricky Master Quest mode could be making a comeback in the new remake.

Dataminer MrCheeze shared a list of strings from the remake's files on Bluesky, several of which tie the tag "MQ" to dungeons like Dodongo's Cavern.

In a follow-up, as spotted by TheGamer, they pointed to further entries, including "HasMQ", "IsMQModeExist", "NewGameMQ", and "ReleaseMQ".

Fellow dataminer OatmealDome added on Twitter/X that the mode will be unlocked by owning DLC, rather than arriving in an update, though "the data is incomplete". "I can confirm that the world is mirrored and dungeons are modified (e.g. cows in Jabu-Jabu's Belly)," they said.

If you've not played it, Master Quest is a remixed version of Ocarina of Time with rearranged dungeons and tougher puzzles. It first appeared as a bonus disc on GameCube, then came back in 2011's Ocarina of Time 3D, which unlocked it after you finished the main game. That version also mirrored the whole world, which matches what OatmealDome has found, and had enemies deal double damage.

[Ocarina of Time] #ootspoilersThere is data in the game files for Master Quest. It will be unlocked by *owning DLC* - it is not just an update.The data is incomplete, but I can confirm that the world is mirrored and dungeons are modified (e.g. cows in Jabu-Jabu's Belly).

As with any datamine, there's no guarantee it'll ever see the light of day. Nintendo hasn't announced any DLC for the remake, and it's not clear whether Master Quest would be free, like it was on 3DS, or paid.

The Ocarina of Time remake launched on Switch 2 on 5th November. Donlan called the new version an "astonishing remake" in his five-star Eurogamer Ocarina of Time review.

Though, to be honest, sometimes I want to play someone else's game.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Skyrim lead designer Bruce Nesmith had a wide-ranging chat with The Examined Game recently, touching upon topics like the importance of institutional knowledge, what he liked about Baldur's Gate 3, and what he wants to see in The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. But he also dropped a pithy maxim (and less pithy explanation) about his—and Bethesda's—approach to design in general. Here's what he said.

"If you look at the history of triple-A studios that do sequels… you'll see the best game in a sequence frequently was able to maintain a vision, and was very player-centric-forward: 'You're not playing my game, I'm making your game' kind of thing.

One of the things I've always felt, and [Bethesda] felt it too [is] once we've made a game, it's not ours anymore. It's yours. I, once upon a time, actually had a developer complain to me that the people playing his game—it wasn't anything Bethesda produced—were playing it wrong.

I immediately told him, 'they're not playing it wrong, they cannot play it wrong, it's their game. It's not yours anymore. However they are choosing to play it is the right way to play it'... If you embrace that on the developer side, you find yourself making all different kinds of content, both artistically and design, and for programming in terms of the systems that are available, so that everyone can play the game the way they want to".

I'm not sure I've ever heard a more succinct summation of the Bethesda school of game design than "You're not playing my game, I'm making your game". Accessibility, openness, a sanding down of edges that may scare off the normies (like ability scores and character classes—gone but not forgotten), and a general refusal to foreclose story branches or quest chains based on player decisions: these things are Bethesda to me.

In this maxim you find all the strengths and weaknesses of the studio's approach to open-world RPG design. On the one hand, the world is your oyster. If a questline is losing your interest, flip to another one. Don't like your build? Convert to something new. Bethesda's worlds are all-you-can-eat buffets and you have precisely zero dietary restrictions. True freedom!

And yet, and yet, to a certain kind of tedious grognard (me), it also leaves everything feeling a touch… limp—colourless in content and utterly unresponsive. You might be the head of every guild in the land and the bloodletter-in-chief of the local murder society, but the world is too shy to reply to it. After all, it can't. If your choices impacted things too hard you might experience a consequence, you might rub up against a rough edge, and then suddenly you might not be playing "your" game anymore.

#3765. Super Smash Bros. Creator Masahiro Sakurai Cautions Against The Use Of Gen AI: ‘We Can Come Up With Better Ideas’

During an event celebrating 40 years of Japanese game magazine Famitsu, Super Smash Bros. supremo Masahiro Sakurai participated in a talk where he discussed his career and work. He shared his thoughts about generative AI, confirming that he has not yet used the technology for any of his current projects, and remains cautious over how useful the tool is in its current state.

The talk was held to coincide with the release of a new book in Japan compiling Sakuraiâs writings for Famitsu magazine. Over the course of the 18 years between 2003 and 2021, Sakurai wrote a column for Famitsu discussing the ever-evolving state of games development and his experience managing the shifting expectations and technologies within the industry. Alongside discussing his past work, the famed game director took some time to address many of the modern concerns facing the industry, including the growing debate surrounding generative AI. At least for now, Sakurai doesn’t think AI can handle tasks in games development or even the brainstorming process, and believes that âwe can come up with better ideas by thinking about them for ourselves.â

âThereâs more [to game development] than simply coming up with an idea,â Sakurai explained. âItâs not enough to just think up an idea. Lots of different factors come into consideration here, like whether you have a fixed deadline or if your team can do it, does it fit into your budget, and so on.â

Currently, Sakurai also believes the technology is not strong enough to even be used for brainstorming ideas, due to the need to factor in the realities of development and the limits on the sort of results it can come up with. He hasnât used it in any of his recent games, including the most recent Kirby Air Raiders, and currently has no plans to use it, doubtful of its capabilities.

That being said, he doesnât rule out its use entirely, as a result of the demands of players and the industry putting increased strain on the development pipeline. According to him, work on Kirby Air Riders was ten times more demanding than it was on the GameCube original, and he notes that there are examples of games unable to turn a profit even after selling millions of units. In order to bring down costs and make these games viable, he suggests the use of AI may be necessary in the future when the technology improves.

âIf you remain stuck on the idea of not using AI because itâs not trustworthy enough as a technology, thereâs a risk that you may fall further and further behind,â Sakurai ponders. âCompared to developers who make games without it, I believe those using AI without hesitation are likely to be able to create more games. As a result, not using may also be a bad idea.â

Developers from Shigeru Miyamoto to Kotaro Uchikoshi have shared varied opinions on the future use cases for AI within the Japanese games industry, and the broad adoption or regulation of AI by Japanese studios. As seen with developers like Sakurai, however, not all are willing to embrace the technology, or feel that generative AI is ready to be trusted with major development tasks.

#3764. COD: Modern Warfare 4 gets a surprisingly sudden free trial, so you can see what the game's extraction mode DMZ is like

Activision has released the first trial for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's extraction mode DMZ. The trial is available across PC (Steam / Battlenet), PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S until Wednesday, 11th November.

The free trial only includes access to DMZ and no other part of Modern Warfare 4, such as multiplayer or the campaign. And while it's not uncommon for Call of Duty titles to make some of their modes available for free for a limited time, the timing of this DMZ taster is notable.

DMZ launched days before Modern Warfare 4's 23rd October release date, meaning this first trial has arrived just two weeks after the game's full launch. By comparison, Black Ops 7's Endgame mode had its first free trial months after launch, in the game's third season. That said, Endgame continued to be freely available until Season 6.

The DMZ trial also coincides with the launch of Modern Warfare 4's iteration of free-to-play Call of Duty battle royale mode Warzone, and Season 1. Indeed, both DMZ and the new Warzone take place on the same Hajin map, so even if you don't decide to buy the full game to continue playing DMZ, some of that map knowledge will certainly transfer to Warzone.

The DMZ trial does not appear to have any limits, meaning you can climb the ranks, access Story Missions - the only way to play PvE, with caveats - and complete Orders to your heart's content. That includes X01, the new endgame dungeon-like area available to experienced and fully-equipped players.

DMZ players who've been asking Infinity Ward to offer a PvE-only playlist of the PvPvE mode will certainly be happy with the influx of new players, as they could potentially amplify their calls for a PvP-free playlist.

#3763. A California airplane got evacuated when a passenger playing Call of Duty was overheard talking about a bomb

You can't just say "bomb" on an airplane.

There really is a proper time and place for things, gamers. Please know that when you’re taking your sweaty callouts into public places.

An avid Call of Duty player reportedly caused their plane to be evacuated last night after they were overheard making callouts, according to CBS News. The Frontier Airlines flight was preparing to take off from Ontario International Airport when a complaint was filed.

The complaint, from another passenger on board, said that they heard someone say words “bomb” and “explosion” and then reported it to the crew. The plane then had to be evacuated and the gamer in question was detained.

The CoD-head was ultimately detained and then had to explain to authorities that “bomb” and “explosion” were used to describe his gameplay, as he was playing the game while on FaceTime with a friend and making callouts mid-match.

I’m normally a big proponent of communication in online games, especially shooters like CoD where teamwork is paramount. Maybe just…not while on an airplane, huh? It’s unclear what CoD game the player was enjoying, but it could’ve been the new Modern Warfare 4 now that it’s portable and playable on the go with Nintendo Switch 2.

And when it comes for saying “bomb” on an airplane, it’s probably not the smartest idea. Traveling is stressful enough and people are on edge, so no matter how silly you may think the other passenger was being, I understand it. Plus, all I can really think of is this one scene from the Ben Stiller/Robert De Niro classic comedy, Meet the Parents:

CBS News said crews swept the plane and found no bomb or explosive device on board, thankfully. There was no word about whether or not the CoD player and his friend won the match in question, although I don’t think the rest of the people on that plane really cared.

Last Friday, the very good RPG Nier: Automata underwent what the scientific community calls 'puffer-fishification'. That is to say, it suddenly and inexplicably ballooned to over 700% of its original download size, as an update magically transformed the game from a reedy 50 GB lightweight into a 366-GB behemoth.

But it has since hit the Ozempic and is now back down to its regular size. "We have identified the cause and now resolved this issue," tweeted the official Nier X account earlier today. "Apologies for any inconvenience caused."

Notably absent from the bugfix notice was any explanation as to just what had happened. It might be academic at this point, but I for one would love to know how you accidentally make a game seven times bigger without anything changing.

Squenix is keeping schtum, but Rick Lane suggested, in our article last week about the bug, that it might have been related to Nier: Automata's DLC packages. "When selected for download on Steam, each DLC appears to have the same file size as the base game", he noted. "Weirdly though, this is only true for the initial download and installation. Once the game is installed, the file reportedly reverts to a more appropriate size of roughly 50 gigs." Indeed, the suggested temporary workaround for the issue (before Square Enix fixed it) was to uncheck all the DLCs when you installed the game.

So it sure seems like, somehow, the base files for the entire original game got attached to each individual DLC package. That might also explain why the size increase only applied to the downloads and not its install size—the whole game got downloaded eight times, but it was simply overwriting the base game files over and over.

That's just my speculation though, and without more news from Squenix, that's all we're gonna get. For now, enjoy being able to once again download 2B and 9S' adventures without having to start the download two weeks in advance.

#3761. GTA 6 reportedly has 55 Achievements/Trophies, more than both GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 had at launch

GTA 6 is due to release on the 19th November on PS5, and Xbox Series X/S, and ahead of the highly-anticipated launch of Rockstar's latest sandbox adventure, people just can't get enough information about the game. To that end, overnight, we saw our latest leak: the game will have 55 Trophies/Achievements.

In a now-deleted tweet from (in)famous Rockstar dataminer, TexFunz2 - re-posted by the Twitter account iGrandTheftAuto - it appears the game will have 55 individual rewards for completing certain tasks and missions. At the time of writing, we don't know specifically what these challenges are, but it seems none of them will be attached to the online version of the game; the base game launches without GTA Online, and so we can safely assume that all these rewards will be for the single-player only content. GTA Online will drop sometime in 2027, according to Twitch's CEO.

If you've been paying attention to previous Rockstar titles, you'll know that Grand Theft Auto 5 launched with 51 Achievements/Trophies - again, all single-player - and Red Dead Redemption 2 launched with 52. So the latest game has more than either game got at launch - and I can tell you from experience, getting Platinum in either title was a very time-consuming experience. Expect the same to be true here, too.

It's worth highlighting that GTA 5 did, eventually, get more Achievements and Trophies: the GTA Online content upped the complete total to 78, adding 27 new challenges to complete. I would expect GTA 6 to do the same… whenever the PC version of GTA comes out, or GTA Online lands in the new game (it's possible both could happen at the same time).

Recently, we heard why a former Rockstar Games tech director thinks GTA 6 could be coming to PC sooner than you'd expect (mostly thanks to AI clones), when we can expect the pre-load of the game (10th November), and how big the final game install is expected to be (210GB). #3760. Sony Announces New Japan-Only PlayStation Portal With Internal Storage

Sony have announced a new Japan-only version of the Playstation Portal, with all-new functionality in the form of internal storage exclusive to the domestic edition of the device.

Last November, Sony released a Japan-only region-locked and language-locked edition of the PS5, reducing the price of this digital-only model from 73,000 ($461) to 55,000 yen ($347). In recent generations, thanks to the success of the Nintendo Switch in Japan and the high cost of PlayStation platforms compared to wages and the cost of living, Sonyâs once-dominant position has diminished. Sony’s Japan-only PS5 aped the decision by Nintendo to create a cheaper, region-specific Nintendo Switch 2. Now Sony is repeating this tactic for the new Japan-only PlayStation Portal, but this time the device appears to be an upgraded version of the hardware.

Although this new PlayStation Portal boasts the same 1080p LCD screen and general features as the worldwide iteration of the device, for this latest version Sony has added internal storage as an all-new feature. Oddly, however, it wonât yet say what it plans to do with this storage. Sony has only said that it “will confirm the future functionality at a later date.” Due to the addition of internal storage, the price of this Japan-only model will be identical to the global model at 39,980 yen ($252), and will be sold in Midnight Black, the same color variant as the Japan-only PS5.

The regular PlayStation Portal can only stream games, either directly from a PlayStation console or via the cloud. The lack of storage prevents games from being downloaded to the device, even though it has its own mobile chipset that, while different to PS5’s, would in theory be capable of running some games locally.

Does this new storage option mean that Sony will enable support for select titles to run natively? Will a similar device with internal storage also be sold internationally? Sony has yet to confirm anything at this time, but considering the success of Portal and the rumors of a next-generation portable, this certainly lends credence to the possibility of a hybrid approach. Pre-orders for the new Japan-only PlayStation Portal begin on Thursday, with a release date planned for December 10.

#3759. Harrison Butker Booed Loudly After Missing Back-to-Back Kicks Amid Controversy

The kicking woes for Harrison Butker and the Kansas City Chiefs are showing no signs of slowing down.

Butker, 31, was loudly booed by the crowd at Kansas City’s Arrowhead Stadium after missing consecutive kicks in the Chiefs’ game against the New York Jets on Sunday, November 8.

Right before halftime, Butker clanged a 56-yard field goal off the upright. After a penalty to the Jets, however, Butker was given a second chance from 51 yards out, which he also missed.

CBS announcer Jim Nantz reacted to the barrage of boos, noting, “The crowd’s letting him have it.”

The Chiefs ultimately won the game, 35-12, putting an end to their two-game losing streak. Butker missed his only field goal attempt of the game, but was five-for-five on extra points.

In the locker room, Butker acknowledged the negative reaction from Chiefs Kingdom.

“I mean, I’m booing myself sometimes,” Butker said. “The fans are passionate. They want [us] to win games. They want me to make kicks. I want to make kicks. I’ve got to be better.”

He added, “I feel confident, I’m excited for the kicks, and I’ve just got to do better. Week after week, saying the same thing. Guys support me. They’ve seen what I’ve done in my 10 seasons, and they want me to be at my best. I know who I can be. I’ve just got to make them go in.”

Butker insisted he’s not dealing with any lingering issues that are causing his dip in accuracy.

“I feel great,” he said. “I definitely have the distance, the power. It’s just making kicks.”

Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes said the team still has “confidence” in Butker, despite his subpar stretch of play.

“That’s pretty much it,” Mahomes, 31, said after the game on Sunday. “I’ve seen him make field goals at the biggest stages that you can make in this league. I want him to know I have as much confidence in him as I’ve ever had, just trying to give him that vote of confidence.”

In response to Butker’s struggles, the Chiefs signed kicker Justin Tucker to their practice squad last month. Tucker, 36, previously served a 10-game suspension for violating the NFL’s personal conduct policy following allegations of sexual misconduct by 16 massage therapists.

Head coach Andy Reid was non-committal about the team’s path forward at the kicking position following the Jets win.

“I’ll address that as we go throughout the week,” Reid, 68, told reporters. “I’ll look at everything. I’m not making any decisions right now.”

The Chiefs travel to Atlanta to play the Falcons on Sunday, November 15.

#3757. Dungeons in World of Warcraft: Forever get a huge XP buff, but power-levellers shouldn't celebrate just yet

World of Warcraft: Forever has received a massive buff to the XP drop-rates of dungeon mobs (enemies), which should make running these instances multiple times feel more rewarding - and may revive an older levelling strategy.

This buff is a 50 percent increase in experience from all mobs killed inside all dungeons. As detailed in this World of Warcraft forum post, community manager Kaivax wrote that this change has been made "so it feels better to go back in for more runs". They don't outright say this is in response to community feedback, but the subject has been a hot topic since the beta.

World of Warcraft: Forever developers have spoken in the past about the decision to deliberately bring down dungeon mob XP to disincentivise power-levelling in dungeons. The idea was that by doing this, people would be encouraged to actually go out into the world and explore it, rather than hopping from instance to instance until they reached max level.

Sadly, a side effect of this change is that doing a dungeon more than once could feel unrewarding. Playing it once is great, as you get to complete lots of quests that reward guaranteed items and XP. However, if you go back again, you don't get these, so your only source of progression comes from a heavily decreased XP rate.

Some quests exacerbate this issue. Dungeons like Wailing Caverns and especially Blackfathom Deeps have a quest that can't really be completed in one run due to a reliance on drop rates for items you need, and having to fight for drops with the rest of your dungeon party. Having to go back to complete this used to suck, and now it sucks less!

So does this mean farming dungeons to power-level is back? Maybe, but it still won't be nearly as efficient as it was in older versions of Classic WoW. The current mob XP rates, after this buff, will still only be 36 percent of the original Classic rate - a third. Given how fast you can level by doing quests out in the world, it seems dungeon farming isn't due for a comeback just yet.

After an especially smooth launch, World of Warcraft: Forever has become the biggest launch in the series' history, beating out Wrath of the Lich King, Cataclysm, and all the other past expansion launches. The developers have been quick to hotfix things on the fly, including a change that left PvP battlegrounds heavily advantaged for the Horde.

I've spent far too much of my life covering the rampant ascent of AI. A juggernaut of tech development, destined to change the world into some sort of sci-fi utopia (if you believe its advocates) or fated to come crashing down around our ears, taking a large chunk of the world economy with it. Or the end of the world as we know it, according to some.

And now, the pillars upon which the AI revolution sits seem to be shaking beneath it. The most recent tremors began with the wobbling of US AI-led tech stocks in mid-October, after a similar descent in China earlier this year. Then at the end of the month, while many tech companies reported huge amounts of revenue in their quarterly financial results, some AI tech share prices still slid under a black cloud of investor doubt.

None more so than Alphabet, the owner of Google. A $500 billion wipe in stock price, led by the admission that the company's own AI search features were eating into its ad revenue, rocked the market. A wider tech sell-off, fuelled by fears regarding the eventual profitability of AI and a potential upcoming Democrat victory in the US midterms, rattled the valuations of many AI tech companies—alongside the chip manufacturers sitting underneath them.

All this, of course, amid a backdrop of increasing AI-related concerns across multiple fields. Rogue AI agents. Increasing AI-powered cybersecurity incidents. Predictions of the end of civilisation, brought on by rampant AI development without proper oversight. Fears of job market ruination. AI psychosis. The list goes on.

Then, the so-called blue wave came to pass. Democrats won control of both the US House and the Senate. Such sweeping political changes can rarely be ascribed to a single factor, but US voter polling indicates that data center expansion was a key source of voter frustration. The current Republican administration has gone all in on AI, and much of the US public seems displeased at the idea of massive AI tech facilities springing up left, right, and center across the country.

Jensen Huang has hit the headlines over allegations surrounding his involvement with an alleged Chinese spy.

Trillions were wiped off US tech stock values as investors sold off increasing numbers of shares in tech companies, amid further fears that the great AI infrastructure buildout was about to be reigned in by political changes. Long-called-for regulation of AI and AI companies seemed—and indeed, still seems—ever more likely.

And now, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has hit the headlines over allegations surrounding his involvement with an alleged Chinese spy. At first, it was reported that Alice Huang (no relation) had a "close relationship" with the Nvidia chief.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Now, Jensen Huang has himself admitted that the two were engaged in an affair, and Nvidia has launched an internal investigation into concerns related to national security. The timing could not be worse for the US tech market. At the time of writing, Nvidia's share value has sunk in pre-market trading.

The company is, in many ways, the backbone of the AI revolution, the chief provider of the chips behind the sweeping AI rollout that has changed the tech landscape over the past few years, and the creator of the CUDA platform that underpins it. Huang is its charismatic leader, the relentless optimist behind this AI-led future we're supposedly about to enjoy. A scandal at this stage is likely the last thing any tech investor wants to see.

So, what now? While the long-mooted AI bubble burst has yet to materialise in full, it's certainly looking like the relentless "all the money in the world" optimism phase is coming to an end. Investors are shaken, with worries about long-term profitability continuing to eat into the market, alongside US national security concerns now dominating the headlines.

The train with no brakes is rocking wildly against the tracks—and unfortunately, given AI and big tech's role in the global economy, we're all stuck in the carriages behind it.

The relentless "all the money in the world" optimism phase is coming to an end.

I'm no economist. I can't tell you if this is the beginning of the AI bubble pop, or whether this is merely an extremely turbulent time in the AI success story. Certainly, it seems like the horse has already bolted, and that AI is here to stay in some form or fashion. Those hoping for a return to the good old, pre-AI days are almost certain to be disappointed.

But, having reported on so many "AI doomsayers" over the past few years, I can tell you that a fall from grace has been predicted by many. Such a massive, world-changing technological development, fuelled by seemingly impossible amounts of investment, has always seemed destined to face some sort of financial reckoning.

That reckoning, I believe, has never looked closer. May you live in interesting times, as the old saying goes. And what happens next? Well, it's going to be interesting, at the very least.

#3755. Complete DREADMOOR Walkthrough: Part 1

DREADMOOR is now out in early access, and it presents an interesting tale for you to explore. Set in a dark, murky world, you have to capture different fish, explore locations, and upgrade your boat.

The campaign of DREADMOOR begins with a tentacle knocking you in the water. The story is broken into multiple quests that you can complete.

The opening will lead you to safe piece of land, and your main objective to get your boat. To do so, you’ll have to power up the generator with the fuel. Once you reach the generator, go to the hut right from there. You’ll find the fuel to power up the generator.

Once the generator has been powered up, you’ll unlock the boat, and then start exploring the world of DREADMOOR. Make sure to pick up the Hook Gun as well along the way.

First, we have to head to the Church Settlement. This place will provide you with your first weapon that allows you to clear blockages. Moreover, you’ll also find the first bed where you can sleep for the night to be over.

Next, we set sail for the Trading Post. Here, we will meet the trader and he will task us with some quest. The trader will also provide us with different blueprints to purchase, but that’s something you can ignore for now.

From there, go upwards to patch the hole in the wall in your shelter. Here, you’ll find the Simple Rod, and you can now fish in the waters. But first, sleep on the bed to survive the night.

Once we get the fishing rod, the next task is to open the door to the Dry Dock. Get the required resources, and then speak with the Engineer to open the doors. This will then allow you to clean and upgrade your ship.

Before you can install the upgrades, you’ll also need to clean the polyps from your ship using the water pipe. Then, you can install the upgrades after crafting them with the required resources. To do so, you’ll have to unlock the blueprints first.

This will complete the first part of the game and get you up to date with all the basics.

#3752. Former NYPD Officer Charged in Fatal Stabbing of Jogger Katie Suarez

A former New York Police Department officer was arrested in connection with the death of Katie Suarez, who was fatally stabbed in the neck while jogging in her Brooklyn neighborhood.

The New York City Police Department confirmed to Us that Sayed Mohassib was arrested on Saturday, November 7, and was charged with murder, tampering with physical evidence and criminal possession of a weapon.

Authorities identified Mohassib, 27, as a suspect after investigators reviewed surveillance footage of the area around the time of the attack, according to NBC News.

The footage allegedly showed Mohassib throwing out trash bags near his residence on the night that Suarez, 28, was killed.

Mohassib allegedly told authorities that he did not remember attacking Suarez though recalled realizing he was covered in blood after the attack, according to NBC News.

It’s not currently clear if Mohassib has entered a plea or retained legal counsel following his arrest. The New York Police Department had no additional updates to share when contacted by Us about the case.

Mohassib was employed as a school aide at an elementary school in Brooklyn at the time of his arrest. A student at the school Mohassib worked at told the New York Post that he was acting “off” in the week leading up to the murder.

“He was acting a little bit, like, I don’t know, weird. A bit off,” the student claimed.

Two other students also spoke to the outlet and claimed that they saw Mohassib talking to himself, while one of the students said that he seemed “nervous” and “worried.”

Following Mohassib’s arrest, the New York City Department of Education confirmed to People that the suspect was an employee of the district.

“The safety of our students is our very top priority,” the representative said in a statement. “We have suspended this individual and will move to terminate employment pending the outcome of the conviction. We are supporting the NYPD in their investigation however is needed.”

The representative added that the department is “providing support and resources to the school community.”

Prior to his role with the school district, Mohassib worked as an employee of the NYPD in 2022. He only served in the role for about a month before requesting to be transferred to the military, a police source told NBC News. The source added that Mohassib was ultimately discharged from military service due to mental health concerns.

Mohassib reportedly requested to rejoin the NYPD in January 2023, but was denied just weeks later.

As Us previously reported, Suarez was jogging on October 30 near a Brooklyn waterfront path on Shore Parkway when she was stabbed two times in the neck around 8:15 p.m. in a seemingly random attack.

Her parents set out to find her when they were unable to get in contact with her, and Suarez was taken to NYU Langone Hospital-Brooklyn for treatment once she was found injured. Suarez succumbed to her injuries three days after the attack.

#3751. "Art, including characters, terrain, animations, cutscenes and UI" Bandai Namco and Monolith Soft helped out with Ocarina of Time on Switch 2

Xenoblade series developer Monolith Soft and Bandai Namco Studios have been listed as support studios for the Switch 2 version of Ocarina of Time, working on elements of the title such as "art, including characters, terrain, animations, cutscenes and UI". Special thanks to both companies appear in the credits for the newly-launched game (as you can see below) and a statement released by Bandai Namco Studios confirms its involvement, too.

"We were commissioned to produce some of the visual assets and artwork, including characters, environments, animations, cutscenes, and UI elements, for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a Nintendo Switch 2 game released by Nintendo Co., Ltd. on 5th November, 2026," reads a translated release from Bandai Namco Studio reads.

Of course, this isn't the first time we've seen Bandai Namco Studios' talents leveraged to help with Nintendo games: the publisher and its internal studios worked closely with Nintendo as a co-developer on the long-awaited Metroid Prime 4, and we know the studios are listed as co-developer for first-party Switch 2 titles like Mario Kart World and Splatoon Raiders. Typically, the work carried out by Bandai Namco comes from one of two dedicated internal studios that are contracted specifically to work with Nintendo: Studio 2 and Studio S. You can see a full list of the games Bandai Namco's support studios have worked on here. You'll note there are many Nintendo first-party titles listed here, going back to 2012 and Mario Kart 8. In late 2025, Nintendo acquired Bandai Namco Studios Singapore from the publisher, renaming the company Nintendo Studios Singapore.

"Alongside great judgement and clever tweaks, this astonishing remake has a proper ace up its sleeve," wrote our reviewer, Christian Donlan, in his five-star review of the Switch 2 game last week. If - somehow! - you've already gobbled up most of the game and you're keen to play it again, you will be pleased to know that Master Quest code has been found in datamined files for the title, suggesting DLC may well be on the way in the not-too-distant future.

#3749. Skyrim lead designer hopes Sentinel will finally solve The Elder Scrolls' ladder problem

For such a simple, straightforward real-world object, ladders have been the bane of game developers' existence since the early days of the industry. And Bethesda's The Elder Scrolls Series is certainly no stranger to that struggle.

While we may be years away from the release of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel, the recent title reveal reignited conversations about what longtime fans hope to see from it. That includes former Bethesda developers, such as Skyrim lead designer and Bethesda veteran Bruce Nesmith, who picked ladders as one thing he hopes Sentinel actually figures out.

If you're unfamiliar, ladders in Skyrim work in a weird way. You don't animatedly climb up and down them, but rather the character simply teleports from one end to the other. Speaking to The Examined Game (via GamesRadar+), Nesmith said that Skyrim's approach "really limits the art team in terms of how you can do multi-layer [levels]".

"It seems simple, it seems stupid, but you don't climb up and down ladders," said Nesmith. "All the ladders in Skyrim, you click on the ladder, poof, you're at the top or you have to climb a stair.

"But to do ladders, you have to deal with a whole host of questions which our programmers very legitimately put in front of us and said, 'You give me answers to these, I'll tell you how much programming time it's going to take to make them.' And you know, that caused problems right there."

Nesmith then pointed out the hidden complexity of creating functioning ladders in games, and the scenarios developers have to anticipate and account for, especially in a game as dynamic as an Elder Scrolls title.

"So, I'm halfway up a ladder, and [an] NPC decides to climb down it. What happens?" Nesmith posited. "The NPC has to have AI that will adjust for that. Does the player go through the NPC? Is he blocked by the NPC? Does the NPC stay on the ladder? Does the NPC go back up and know to wait and then come back down?

"And I'm just scratching the surface of some of the problems they brought up. So, it seems simple, and other games have climbing ladders, but we chose to put our efforts into other things to make them better rather than deal with that. So, I'd like to see Bethesda finally come around to making ladders a reality where you're actually climbing them and make the world feel a little more immersive."

While we know very little about Sentinel right now - much less how it's going to solve the ladder problem -that hasn't stopped fans from speculating about a number of topics, including what they believe is going to be a split / alternate timeline setup.

#3748. Ex–PlayStation Exec Says True Innovation Would Be Making The PS6 Cheaper: ‘We Have Enough Power In The Machine’

PlayStation 6 is coming and it’s not coming cheaply. Sony is making “solid progress in preparing for the next-generation platform,” the company said last week, but its next-gen device is also reportedly likely to cost over $1,000. ExâPlayStation executive Shawn Layden would prefer the PS6 innovate on price rather than power.

“I think we have enough power in the machine,” the former chairman of SIE Worldwide Studios told The Trophy Room in a recent interview. “The innovation needs to come not from making PS6 for $1,200âit’s to make another PS5 for $300. Now, that would be true innovation.”

Layden has been a critic of the console war arms race in recent years, arguing that improvements have become increasingly hard to spot with the naked eye while sitting in anything less than pristine viewing conditions. The price tags for these improvements have also skyrocketed. Not only has the price of the PS5 actually gone up during its life cycle, the budgets for triple-A studios have exploded even as sales stay flat or go down, leading to a crisis among big publishers.

“I mean, the the jump from PS1 to PS2 was incredible, right?” he said. “And the jump from compact disc to DVD, different storage medium, higher density, and then from two to three when you got to 1080p and you can really do 60 frames per second at uh, you know, at a high frame rate. And then PS4, which was like, [it] completely worked and all that was done and and you still got it for $399. And then PS5, we’re talking about ray tracing and teraflops. And the talk about PS6 is even more ray tracing and more teraflops. These are the differences only dogs can hear.”

These trends are also coming to a head at a time when AI hyperscalers are consuming RAM at an unprecedented clip, spiking the prices for other hardware manufacturers at an unsustainable pace. Some companies predict the prices will only continue to go up through 2028, meaning the next generation of consoles could be the least affordable and the least impressive relative to the sorts of performance leaps fans have been trained to expect from a new batch of hardware.

Then you look at the Switch 2 and Steam and realize that millions of gamers are content just to play great games, regardless of whether they are graphical showcases or not. Lots of us just spent the weekend playing the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. I had plenty of thoughts strolling down memory lane but “I wish this looked better” definitely wasn’t one of them.

#3746. Nintendo's legendary Kirby designer Masahiro Sakurai weighs in on gen-AI, saying "it has yet to gain my trust" but not to reject it completely

"Doing nothing is probably not the right approach."

Masahiro Sakurai, the designer behind many iconic Nintendo franchises such as Super Smash Bros. and several Kirby titles, has weighed in on the ongoing discussion of generative-AI use in game development.

At an event celebrating the release of his new book - Masahiro Sakurai’s Thoughts on Games - the veteran director told Famitsu he hasn't and currently isn't using the technology to make games, noting that the role of a designer is to generate ideas.

"It has yet to gain my trust," Sakurai said via DeepL machine translation. Regarding graphical use specifically, he added that, "It must not amount to exploitation of any kind," and that "for the time being, we can produce better results by coming up with ideas ourselves".

But Sakurai is wary of rejecting gen-AI completely, saying "making games today is far too difficult", with some games "running at a loss even after selling millions of copies". A company in that position may go under if it does not change its stance on generative-AI, he suggested. "Doing nothing is probably not the right approach," he said, but "where and how to use it" is a complex topic with a lot of uncertainties. Sakurai is taking "a slow-paced approach" for now.

Outside of regular industry layoffs, the use of generative-AI in games has been the most controversial topic amongst developers and players. Some argue it's already being used in multiple development disciplines, notably programming and writing code. Others, such as Shigeru Miyamoto, are more sceptical of the technology's capabilities, especially when it comes to the more creative and art-driven parts of game development.
